Artificial Intelligence Research - Language Model Training from Scratch
Lesson 06: Language Model Training from Scratch
Introduction
Language models are the foundation of modern NLP. Understanding how to build one from scratch — from raw text to a working GPT-style model — is essential knowledge for any AI researcher. This lesson walks through every step: tokenization, vocabulary construction, the transformer architecture with causal attention masking, the next-token prediction objective, and training on custom corpora.
1. Tokenization
1.1 Why Tokenize?
Neural networks operate on numbers, not text. Tokenization converts text into a sequence of integer IDs. The choice of tokenizer affects vocabulary size, sequence length, and model performance.
"The quick brown fox" -> [464, 2068, 7586, 21831]  (BPE tokens)
1.2 Tokenization Methods
Method | Description | Used By
Word-level | One token per word | Older models (Word2Vec)
Character-level | One token per character | Very small vocab, long sequences
BPE (Byte-Pair Encoding) | Iteratively merge frequent pairs | GPT-2, GPT-3, Llama
WordPiece | Similar to BPE, likelihood-based | BERT, DistilBERT
Unigram | Remove tokens that least affect likelihood | SentencePiece, T5
Byte-level BPE | BPE on raw bytes (no unknown tokens) | GPT-2, Llama
1.3 BPE (Byte-Pair Encoding) Algorithm
Step 1: Start with character-level vocabulary  "low" -> ['l', 'o', 'w']  "lower" -> ['l', 'o', 'w', 'e', 'r']  "newest" -> ['n', 'e', 'w', 'e', 's', 't']Step 2: Count all adjacent pairs  ('l','o'): 2, ('o','w'): 2, ('w','e'): 2, ('e','r'): 1, ...Step 3: Merge most frequent pair -> ('l','o') => 'lo'  "low" -> ['lo', 'w']  "lower" -> ['lo', 'w', 'e', 'r']Step 4: Repeat until desired vocabulary size
def train_bpe(texts, vocab_size=1000):    """Simple BPE training implementation."""    # Start with character vocabulary    from collections import Counter    # Count word frequencies    word_freqs = Counter()    for text in texts:        for word in text.split():            word_freqs[' '.join(list(word)) + ' </w>'] += 1    # Get initial vocabulary    vocab = set()    for word in word_freqs:        for char in word.split():            vocab.add(char)    merges = []    while len(vocab) < vocab_size:        # Count pairs        pairs = Counter()        for word, freq in word_freqs.items():            symbols = word.split()            for i in range(len(symbols) - 1):                pairs[(symbols[i], symbols[i+1])] += freq        if not pairs:            break        # Find most frequent pair        best_pair = max(pairs, key=pairs.get)        merges.append(best_pair)        vocab.add(''.join(best_pair))        # Apply merge        new_word_freqs = {}        bigram = ' '.join(best_pair)        replacement = ''.join(best_pair)        for word, freq in word_freqs.items():            new_word = word.replace(bigram, replacement)            new_word_freqs[new_word] = freq        word_freqs = new_word_freqs    return vocab, merges
1.4 Training a Tokenizer with Hugging Face
from tokenizers import Tokenizer, models, trainers, pre_tokenizers# Create a BPE tokenizertokenizer = Tokenizer(models.BPE())tokenizer.pre_tokenizer = pre_tokenizers.ByteLevel(add_prefix_space=False)trainer = trainers.BpeTrainer(    vocab_size=32000,    special_tokens=["<pad>", "<bos>", "<eos>", "<unk>"],    min_frequency=2,)# Train on your corpustokenizer.train(files=["corpus.txt"], trainer=trainer)# Use itencoded = tokenizer.encode("Hello, world!")print(encoded.ids)      # [15496, 11, 995, 0]print(encoded.tokens)   # ['Hello', ',', 'Ġworld', '!']
1.5 SentencePiece
SentencePiece treats the input as raw text (including whitespace), making it language-agnostic:
import sentencepiece as spm# Trainspm.SentencePieceTrainer.train(    input='corpus.txt',    model_prefix='my_tokenizer',    vocab_size=32000,    model_type='bpe',  # or 'unigram')# Load and usesp = spm.SentencePieceProcessor()sp.load('my_tokenizer.model')tokens = sp.encode("Hello world", out_type=str)ids = sp.encode("Hello world", out_type=int)text = sp.decode(ids)
Key Insight: The choice of vocabulary size is a tradeoff. Smaller vocabularies (8K-16K) lead to longer sequences but better handling of rare words. Larger vocabularies (32K-64K) give shorter sequences but may waste capacity on rare tokens. For most LLM work, 32K is a good default.
2. Building a GPT-Style Model
2.1 Architecture Overview
GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) uses a decoder-only transformer with causal (unidirectional) attention:
Input Tokens:  [The] [cat] [sat] [on]                 |     |     |     |Token Embedding + Positional Encoding                 |     |     |     |       +---------|-----|-----|-----|--------+       |    Causal Self-Attention (masked)  |       |    + Feed-Forward Network          | x N layers       |    + Layer Norm + Residual         |       +---------|-----|-----|-----|--------+                 |     |     |     |             [Linear + Softmax]                 |     |     |     |             Predict next token:             [cat] [sat] [on] [the]
2.2 Causal Attention Masking
In causal (autoregressive) attention, each token can only attend to previous tokens and itself:
Attention Matrix (before softmax):         The  cat  sat  onThe    [  x   -inf -inf -inf ]cat    [  x    x   -inf -inf ]sat    [  x    x    x   -inf ]on     [  x    x    x    x   ]x = computed attention score-inf = masked (cannot attend to future tokens)
2.3 Core Components
import torchimport torch.nn as nnimport torch.nn.functional as Fimport mathclass CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):    """Multi-head causal (masked) self-attention."""    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, max_seq_len, dropout=0.1):        super().__init__()        assert d_model % n_heads == 0        self.n_heads = n_heads        self.d_head = d_model // n_heads        self.d_model = d_model        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model)        self.proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)        self.attn_dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)        self.proj_dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)        # Causal mask        self.register_buffer(            "mask",            torch.tril(torch.ones(max_seq_len, max_seq_len)).view(1, 1, max_seq_len, max_seq_len)        )    def forward(self, x):        B, T, C = x.shape        # Compute Q, K, V        qkv = self.qkv(x)  # (B, T, 3*C)        q, k, v = qkv.split(self.d_model, dim=2)        # Reshape for multi-head attention        q = q.view(B, T, self.n_heads, self.d_head).transpose(1, 2)        k = k.view(B, T, self.n_heads, self.d_head).transpose(1, 2)        v = v.view(B, T, self.n_heads, self.d_head).transpose(1, 2)        # Attention scores        attn = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(self.d_head)        # Apply causal mask        attn = attn.masked_fill(self.mask[:, :, :T, :T] == 0, float('-inf'))        # Softmax and dropout        attn = F.softmax(attn, dim=-1)        attn = self.attn_dropout(attn)        # Apply attention to values        out = attn @ v  # (B, n_heads, T, d_head)        out = out.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, T, C)        return self.proj_dropout(self.proj(out))
2.4 Feed-Forward Network
class FeedForward(nn.Module):    """Position-wise feed-forward network with GELU activation."""    def __init__(self, d_model, d_ff=None, dropout=0.1):        super().__init__()        d_ff = d_ff or 4 * d_model        self.net = nn.Sequential(            nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff),            nn.GELU(),            nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model),            nn.Dropout(dropout),        )    def forward(self, x):        return self.net(x)
2.5 Transformer Block
class TransformerBlock(nn.Module):    """A single transformer decoder block."""    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, max_seq_len, dropout=0.1):        super().__init__()        self.ln1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)        self.attn = CausalSelfAttention(d_model, n_heads, max_seq_len, dropout)        self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)        self.ff = FeedForward(d_model, dropout=dropout)    def forward(self, x):        x = x + self.attn(self.ln1(x))  # Pre-norm residual        x = x + self.ff(self.ln2(x))        return x
Note: We use pre-norm (LayerNorm before the sublayer) rather than post-norm (after the sublayer). Pre-norm is the standard for modern transformers because it leads to more stable training and allows the model to be trained without careful warmup.
2.6 Complete GPT Model
class MiniGPT(nn.Module):    """A small GPT-style language model."""    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_model=256, n_heads=8, n_layers=6,                 max_seq_len=512, dropout=0.1):        super().__init__()        self.token_emb = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)        self.pos_emb = nn.Embedding(max_seq_len, d_model)        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)        self.blocks = nn.Sequential(*[            TransformerBlock(d_model, n_heads, max_seq_len, dropout)            for _ in range(n_layers)        ])        self.ln_f = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)        self.head = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size, bias=False)        # Weight tying        self.token_emb.weight = self.head.weight        self.max_seq_len = max_seq_len        self.apply(self._init_weights)    def _init_weights(self, module):        if isinstance(module, nn.Linear):            nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.02)            if module.bias is not None:                nn.init.zeros_(module.bias)        elif isinstance(module, nn.Embedding):            nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.02)    def forward(self, idx, targets=None):        B, T = idx.shape        assert T <= self.max_seq_len        # Embeddings        tok_emb = self.token_emb(idx)        pos_emb = self.pos_emb(torch.arange(T, device=idx.device))        x = self.dropout(tok_emb + pos_emb)        # Transformer blocks        x = self.blocks(x)        x = self.ln_f(x)        # Language model head        logits = self.head(x)  # (B, T, vocab_size)        loss = None        if targets is not None:            loss = F.cross_entropy(                logits.view(-1, logits.size(-1)),                targets.view(-1),                ignore_index=-1            )        return logits, loss    @torch.no_grad()    def generate(self, idx, max_new_tokens, temperature=1.0, top_k=None):        """Autoregressive generation."""        for _ in range(max_new_tokens):            # Crop to max_seq_len            idx_cond = idx[:, -self.max_seq_len:]            # Forward pass            logits, _ = self(idx_cond)            logits = logits[:, -1, :] / temperature            # Optional top-k filtering            if top_k is not None:                v, _ = torch.topk(logits, min(top_k, logits.size(-1)))                logits[logits < v[:, [-1]]] = float('-inf')            probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)            idx_next = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1)            idx = torch.cat([idx, idx_next], dim=1)        return idx
3. The Next-Token Prediction Objective
3.1 Causal Language Modeling (CLM)
Given a sequence of tokens [t1, t2, ..., tn], the model learns to predict each next token:
Input:  [The]  [cat]  [sat]  [on]   [the]Target: [cat]  [sat]  [on]   [the]  [mat]Loss = -1/N * sum(log P(t_{i+1} | t_1, ..., t_i))
3.2 Perplexity
Perplexity is the standard evaluation metric for language models:
Perplexity = exp(average cross-entropy loss)           = exp(-1/N * sum(log P(t_i | t_1, ..., t_{i-1})))
Lower perplexity = better model. A perplexity of K means the model is as uncertain as choosing uniformly from K options.
Model | Perplexity (WikiText-103)
Random (vocab 32K) | 32,000
N-gram (Kneser-Ney) | ~150
LSTM | ~65
GPT-2 Small | ~30
GPT-2 XL | ~18
Key Insight: The beauty of next-token prediction is its simplicity and scalability. You need no labeled data — any text is training data. The objective forces the model to learn grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, and even some degree of common sense, all through the seemingly simple task of predicting the next word.
4. Training on Custom Corpora
4.1 Data Preparation
class TextDataset(Dataset):    """Dataset for language model training."""    def __init__(self, text, tokenizer, block_size=512):        self.block_size = block_size        # Tokenize entire text        self.tokens = tokenizer.encode(text)        print(f"Total tokens: {len(self.tokens):,}")    def __len__(self):        return max(0, len(self.tokens) - self.block_size - 1)    def __getitem__(self, idx):        chunk = self.tokens[idx: idx + self.block_size + 1]        x = torch.tensor(chunk[:-1], dtype=torch.long)        y = torch.tensor(chunk[1:], dtype=torch.long)        return x, y
4.2 Training Loop
def train_lm(model, train_loader, optimizer, scheduler, device, epochs=10):    model.train()    for epoch in range(epochs):        total_loss = 0        for batch_idx, (x, y) in enumerate(train_loader):            x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)            logits, loss = model(x, targets=y)            optimizer.zero_grad()            loss.backward()            torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)            optimizer.step()            scheduler.step()            total_loss += loss.item()        avg_loss = total_loss / len(train_loader)        ppl = math.exp(avg_loss)        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}: Loss={avg_loss:.4f}, Perplexity={ppl:.2f}")
5. Weight Tying
5.1 What and Why
Weight tying shares the token embedding matrix with the output projection (language model head):
# In the model:self.token_emb = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)self.head = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size, bias=False)self.token_emb.weight = self.head.weight  # Tie weights
Benefits:
* Reduces parameter count significantly (vocab_size * d_model parameters saved)
* Improves performance — the model learns better token representations
* Standard practice in all modern language models
6. Positional Encoding
6.1 Learned vs. Sinusoidal
Method | Description | Used By
Sinusoidal | Fixed sin/cos functions | Original Transformer
Learned | Trainable embedding table | GPT-2, BERT
RoPE | Rotary Position Embedding | Llama, Mistral
ALiBi | Attention with Linear Biases | BLOOM
6.2 RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding)
RoPE encodes position by rotating the query and key vectors:
class RotaryPositionEmbedding(nn.Module):    def __init__(self, dim, max_seq_len=2048):        super().__init__()        inv_freq = 1.0 / (10000 ** (torch.arange(0, dim, 2).float() / dim))        self.register_buffer("inv_freq", inv_freq)        t = torch.arange(max_seq_len).float()        freqs = torch.einsum("i,j->ij", t, inv_freq)        emb = torch.cat([freqs, freqs], dim=-1)        self.register_buffer("cos", emb.cos())        self.register_buffer("sin", emb.sin())    def forward(self, x, seq_len):        return self.cos[:seq_len], self.sin[:seq_len]def apply_rotary_emb(x, cos, sin):    """Apply rotary embeddings to queries and keys."""    d = x.shape[-1]    x1, x2 = x[..., :d//2], x[..., d//2:]    rotated = torch.cat([-x2, x1], dim=-1)    return x * cos + rotated * sin
Key Insight: RoPE has become the dominant positional encoding for modern LLMs because it naturally supports relative position encoding, extrapolates to longer sequences than seen during training (with some fidelity loss), and integrates cleanly with attention computation.

* Experiment with model size: Train models with 2, 4, 8, and 16 layers. Plot perplexity vs. parameters.
* Add RoPE: Replace learned positional embeddings with RoPE. Compare on sequences longer than training length.
* Train a domain-specific LM: Train on code, medical text, or legal documents. Evaluate domain-specific perplexity.
8. Summary
Concept | Key Takeaway
Tokenization | BPE is the standard; 32K vocabulary is a good default
Causal Attention | Each token sees only past tokens; implemented via upper-triangular mask
Next-Token Prediction | Simple but powerful; forces learning of language structure
Perplexity | exp(loss); lower is better; the standard LM metric
Weight Tying | Share embedding and output weights; reduces params, improves performance
Positional Encoding | RoPE is the modern standard for decoder-only models
Pre-norm | LayerNorm before sublayers; more stable training

Artificial Intelligence Research - Distributed Training and Scalability
Lesson 07: Distributed Training and Scalability
Introduction
Training modern deep learning models often requires distributing computation across multiple GPUs or even multiple machines. A single GPU cannot hold or train a large language model in reasonable time. This lesson covers the full spectrum of distributed training: from data parallelism (the simplest) to model parallelism, pipeline parallelism, and advanced frameworks like DeepSpeed and FSDP. We also cover mixed precision training, which can double throughput with minimal accuracy impact.
1. Why Distributed Training?
1.1 The Scale Problem
Model | Parameters | Memory (FP32) | Training Compute
ResNet-50 | 25M | 100 MB | 1 GPU-day
GPT-2 | 1.5B | 6 GB | ~256 GPU-days
Llama 2 7B | 7B | 28 GB | ~200K GPU-hours
Llama 2 70B | 70B | 280 GB | ~1.7M GPU-hours
GPT-4 (est.) | ~1.7T | ~7 TB | ~25K A100 for 3 months
1.2 Memory Breakdown
For a model with P parameters, training requires memory for:
Total Memory = Model Params + Gradients + Optimizer States + ActivationsFP32 Training:  Params:          4 * P bytes  Gradients:       4 * P bytes  Adam states:     8 * P bytes (momentum + variance)  ---  Subtotal:        16 * P bytes (without activations)Example (7B model):  16 * 7B = 112 GB (just for params + optimizer!)  + Activations (depends on batch size and sequence length)
Key Insight: A 7B parameter model requires at least 112 GB of GPU memory in FP32 just for parameters and optimizer states — far more than a single GPU's capacity (A100: 80 GB). Distributed training and memory optimization are not optional at this scale; they are fundamental requirements.
2. Data Parallelism (DDP)
2.1 Concept
Data Parallelism is the simplest form of distributed training: replicate the model on each GPU, split the data, and average gradients.
Data: [Batch 1] [Batch 2] [Batch 3] [Batch 4]              |          |          |          |           GPU 0      GPU 1      GPU 2      GPU 3           (copy)     (copy)     (copy)     (copy)              |          |          |          |         Forward    Forward    Forward    Forward         Backward   Backward   Backward   Backward              |          |          |          |              +-----AllReduce(gradients)------+              |          |          |          |          Update     Update     Update     Update
2.2 PyTorch DDP
import torchimport torch.distributed as distimport torch.nn as nnfrom torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDPfrom torch.utils.data.distributed import DistributedSamplerimport osdef setup(rank, world_size):    """Initialize the distributed process group."""    os.environ['MASTER_ADDR'] = 'localhost'    os.environ['MASTER_PORT'] = '12355'    dist.init_process_group("nccl", rank=rank, world_size=world_size)    torch.cuda.set_device(rank)def cleanup():    dist.destroy_process_group()def train_ddp(rank, world_size, model_class, dataset, num_epochs=10):    setup(rank, world_size)    # Create model and wrap with DDP    model = model_class().to(rank)    model = DDP(model, device_ids=[rank])    # Distributed sampler ensures each GPU gets different data    sampler = DistributedSampler(dataset, num_replicas=world_size, rank=rank)    loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=32, sampler=sampler, num_workers=4)    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()    for epoch in range(num_epochs):        sampler.set_epoch(epoch)  # Crucial for proper shuffling        model.train()        for inputs, targets in loader:            inputs = inputs.to(rank)            targets = targets.to(rank)            optimizer.zero_grad()            outputs = model(inputs)            loss = criterion(outputs, targets)            loss.backward()  # DDP automatically syncs gradients            optimizer.step()    cleanup()# Launch with:# torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 script.py
2.3 torchrun Launch
# Single node, 4 GPUstorchrun --nproc_per_node=4 train_ddp.py# Multi-node (node 0)torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 --nnodes=2 --node_rank=0 \    --master_addr=10.0.0.1 --master_port=12355 train_ddp.py# Multi-node (node 1)torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 --nnodes=2 --node_rank=1 \    --master_addr=10.0.0.1 --master_port=12355 train_ddp.py
Note: torchrun (replacing the older torch.distributed.launch) handles spawning processes, setting environment variables (RANK, LOCAL_RANK, WORLD_SIZE), and fault tolerance with elastic training.
3. Model Parallelism
3.1 Tensor Parallelism
Splits individual layers across GPUs. A linear layer W of size (d, d) is split into shards:
Tensor Parallelism (column split):   Input X (B, d)       |   +---+---+   |       |GPU 0:   GPU 1:W[:,:d/2] W[:,d/2:]   |       |   Y_0     Y_1   |       |   +---+---+       |   Y = [Y_0, Y_1]   (concatenate)
Megatron-LM style tensor parallelism for attention:
# Conceptual: split heads across GPUsclass TensorParallelAttention(nn.Module):    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, tp_size):        super().__init__()        # Each GPU handles n_heads // tp_size heads        self.local_heads = n_heads // tp_size        self.local_d = d_model // tp_size        self.q = nn.Linear(d_model, self.local_d, bias=False)        self.k = nn.Linear(d_model, self.local_d, bias=False)        self.v = nn.Linear(d_model, self.local_d, bias=False)        self.proj = nn.Linear(self.local_d, d_model, bias=False)
3.2 Pipeline Parallelism
Splits the model into stages, each on a different GPU. Uses micro-batches to keep GPUs busy:
Time ->        Micro-batch 1  Micro-batch 2  Micro-batch 3  Micro-batch 4GPU 0:  [Stage 1 Fwd]  [Stage 1 Fwd]  [Stage 1 Fwd]  [Stage 1 Fwd]GPU 1:     idle         [Stage 2 Fwd]  [Stage 2 Fwd]  [Stage 2 Fwd]GPU 2:     idle            idle         [Stage 3 Fwd]  [Stage 3 Fwd]GPU 3:     idle            idle            idle         [Stage 4 Fwd]Then backward pass in reverse...The "bubble" (idle time) is minimized by using many micro-batches.Bubble fraction ≈ (num_stages - 1) / num_micro_batches
3.3 3D Parallelism
Modern LLM training combines all three:
Tensor Parallelism (within a layer)                    +------+------+------+------+                    |GPU 0 |GPU 1 |GPU 2 |GPU 3 | <-- Layer heads split across 4 GPUsPipeline            +------+------+------+------+Parallelism         |GPU 4 |GPU 5 |GPU 6 |GPU 7 | <-- Next pipeline stage(across layers)     +------+------+------+------+                    |GPU 8 |GPU 9 |GPU10 |GPU11 |                    +------+------+------+------+Data Parallelism: Replicate the above across multiple nodes
4. ZeRO Optimization
4.1 ZeRO Stages
ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer) partitions optimizer states, gradients, and parameters across GPUs:
ZeRO Stage | What is Partitioned | Memory per GPU | Communication
Stage 0 | Nothing (standard DDP) | 16P / N + 16P | AllReduce
Stage 1 | Optimizer states | 4P + 12P/N | AllReduce
Stage 2 | + Gradients | 4P + (4+8)P/N | Reduce-Scatter
Stage 3 | + Parameters | 16P/N | All-Gather
Where N is the number of GPUs and P is the parameter count.
Standard DDP (4 GPUs, 1B params):  Each GPU: 16 GB (full model + optimizer)  Total: 64 GBZeRO Stage 3 (4 GPUs, 1B params):  Each GPU: 4 GB (1/4 of everything)  Total: 16 GB (same as 1 GPU, but distributed!)
Key Insight: ZeRO Stage 3 enables training models that are N times larger than what fits on a single GPU, where N is the number of GPUs. This is a game-changer for research groups with modest hardware. A cluster of 8 GPUs with 24 GB each can train a model that would require 192 GB on a single GPU.
5. FSDP (Fully Sharded Data Parallel)
5.1 Overview
FSDP is PyTorch's native implementation of ZeRO Stage 3. It shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across GPUs:
from torch.distributed.fsdp import FullyShardedDataParallel as FSDPfrom torch.distributed.fsdp import ShardingStrategy, MixedPrecision# Wrap model with FSDPfsdp_model = FSDP(    model,    sharding_strategy=ShardingStrategy.FULL_SHARD,  # ZeRO-3 equivalent    mixed_precision=MixedPrecision(        param_dtype=torch.bfloat16,        reduce_dtype=torch.bfloat16,        buffer_dtype=torch.bfloat16,    ),    auto_wrap_policy=size_based_auto_wrap_policy,    device_id=torch.cuda.current_device(),)
5.2 Wrapping Policy
from torch.distributed.fsdp.wrap import size_based_auto_wrap_policy, transformer_auto_wrap_policyfrom functools import partial# Option 1: Wrap layers above a parameter thresholdauto_wrap = partial(size_based_auto_wrap_policy, min_num_params=1e6)# Option 2: Wrap specific module types (better for transformers)auto_wrap = partial(    transformer_auto_wrap_policy,    transformer_layer_cls={TransformerBlock},)
6. DeepSpeed
6.1 Overview
DeepSpeed (by Microsoft) provides ZeRO optimization, pipeline parallelism, and many training optimizations:
import deepspeed# Initializemodel, optimizer, _, scheduler = deepspeed.initialize(    model=model,    model_parameters=model.parameters(),    config="ds_config.json",)# Training loop (simplified)for batch in train_loader:    loss = model(batch)    model.backward(loss)    model.step()
6.2 DeepSpeed Configuration
{    "train_batch_size": 256,    "gradient_accumulation_steps": 4,    "optimizer": {        "type": "AdamW",        "params": {            "lr": 3e-4,            "weight_decay": 0.01,            "betas": [0.9, 0.95]        }    },    "scheduler": {        "type": "WarmupDecayLR",        "params": {            "warmup_min_lr": 0,            "warmup_max_lr": 3e-4,            "warmup_num_steps": 1000,            "total_num_steps": 100000        }    },    "fp16": {        "enabled": true,        "loss_scale": 0,        "loss_scale_window": 1000    },    "zero_optimization": {        "stage": 2,        "offload_optimizer": {            "device": "cpu",            "pin_memory": true        },        "allgather_partitions": true,        "allgather_bucket_size": 5e8,        "reduce_scatter": true,        "reduce_bucket_size": 5e8,        "overlap_comm": true,        "contiguous_gradients": true    },    "gradient_clipping": 1.0,    "wall_clock_breakdown": false}
6.3 DeepSpeed ZeRO-Offload
ZeRO-Offload moves optimizer states and gradients to CPU memory, enabling training of larger models:
GPU Memory: Model parameters + activationsCPU Memory: Optimizer states + gradientsCPU Compute: Optimizer update stepThis allows training a 10B model on a single GPU!(At the cost of slower training due to CPU-GPU data transfer)
7. Mixed Precision Training
7.1 Floating Point Formats
Format | Bits | Exponent | Mantissa | Range | Precision
FP32 | 32 | 8 | 23 | 3.4e38 | ~7 digits
FP16 | 16 | 5 | 10 | 6.5e4 | ~3.3 digits
BF16 | 16 | 8 | 7 | 3.4e38 | ~2.4 digits
FP8 (E4M3) | 8 | 4 | 3 | 448 | ~1 digit
FP8 (E5M2) | 8 | 5 | 2 | 57344 | ~0.6 digit
7.2 Why Mixed Precision?
FP32: 4 bytes/param -> Slower, more memoryFP16: 2 bytes/param -> 2x faster, half memory, BUT can overflow/underflowBF16: 2 bytes/param -> Same range as FP32, less precision, simpler to use
7.3 PyTorch Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP)
from torch.cuda.amp import autocast, GradScalerscaler = GradScaler()  # Handles loss scaling for FP16for inputs, targets in train_loader:    optimizer.zero_grad()    # Forward pass in mixed precision    with autocast(dtype=torch.float16):        outputs = model(inputs)        loss = criterion(outputs, targets)    # Backward with scaled loss (prevents gradient underflow)    scaler.scale(loss).backward()    # Unscale gradients before clipping    scaler.unscale_(optimizer)    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)    # Optimizer step with scaler    scaler.step(optimizer)    scaler.update()
7.4 BF16 (Simpler)
BFloat16 has the same exponent range as FP32, so it does not need loss scaling:
# BF16 is simpler — no scaler neededwith autocast(dtype=torch.bfloat16):    outputs = model(inputs)    loss = criterion(outputs, targets)loss.backward()optimizer.step()
Key Insight: BF16 is the recommended precision for modern GPU training (A100, H100). It offers 2x speedup and memory savings without the complexity of FP16 loss scaling. FP16 is still useful for older GPUs (V100) that lack BF16 hardware support.
8. Gradient Checkpointing
8.1 The Memory-Compute Tradeoff
Gradient checkpointing saves memory by recomputing activations during the backward pass instead of storing them:
Without checkpointing:  Forward:  Store activations at every layer  Backward: Use stored activations to compute gradients  Memory:   O(N) where N = number of layersWith checkpointing:  Forward:  Store activations only at checkpoint layers  Backward: Recompute activations from nearest checkpoint  Memory:   O(sqrt(N))  Compute:  ~33% more (one extra forward pass per segment)
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpointclass CheckpointedTransformerBlock(nn.Module):    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):        super().__init__()        self.attn = SelfAttention(d_model, n_heads)        self.ff = FeedForward(d_model)        self.ln1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)        self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)    def forward(self, x):        # Checkpoint the attention and FFN computations        x = x + checkpoint(self.attn, self.ln1(x), use_reentrant=False)        x = x + checkpoint(self.ff, self.ln2(x), use_reentrant=False)        return x
9. Communication Backends
9.1 Backend Comparison
Backend | GPU Support | CPU Support | Best For
NCCL | Yes | No | GPU-to-GPU (default for CUDA)
Gloo | Yes | Yes | CPU training, fallback
MPI | Depends | Yes | HPC clusters
9.2 Communication Operations
AllReduce:   Every GPU sends and receives the sum of all gradients             O(data_size) communication per GPUAllGather:   Every GPU sends its shard and receives all shards             O(data_size * N) totalReduceScatter: Reduce and distribute different chunks to different GPUs               O(data_size) communicationBroadcast:   One GPU sends data to all others             O(data_size) communication
10. Practical Distributed Training Checklist
1. Start Simple:   [ ] Begin with DDP (single node, multi-GPU)   [ ] Verify training matches single-GPU baseline2. Scale Up:   [ ] Add mixed precision (BF16 preferred)   [ ] Add gradient checkpointing if memory-constrained   [ ] Use FSDP or DeepSpeed ZeRO if model doesn't fit in GPU3. Multi-Node:   [ ] Set up NCCL communication   [ ] Use torchrun for launching   [ ] Monitor network bandwidth utilization4. Debugging:   [ ] Check that all ranks produce the same loss at step 0   [ ] Verify gradient synchronization with dist.all_reduce   [ ] Use NCCL_DEBUG=INFO for communication debugging
11. Exercises
* DDP training: Convert a single-GPU training script to DDP. Verify identical results.
* Mixed precision: Add AMP to an existing script. Measure speedup and memory savings.
* FSDP: Wrap a large model with FSDP. Compare memory usage to DDP.
* DeepSpeed: Configure ZeRO Stage 2 for an existing model.
* Gradient checkpointing: Enable checkpointing and measure the memory-compute tradeoff.
12. Summary
Technique | What It Does | When to Use
DDP | Replicates model, averages gradients | Default for multi-GPU
Tensor Parallelism | Splits layers across GPUs | Very large layers
Pipeline Parallelism | Splits model stages across GPUs | Very deep models
ZeRO / FSDP | Shards optimizer/gradients/params | Model too large for one GPU
Mixed Precision | Half-precision compute | Always (for speed)
Gradient Checkpointing | Recompute activations | Memory-constrained
DeepSpeed | Framework with ZeRO + optimizations | LLM training

Artificial Intelligence Research - Training Large Language Models
Lesson 08: Training Large Language Models
Introduction
Training large language models (LLMs) is one of the most challenging engineering and scientific problems in modern AI. It involves managing trillion-token datasets, maintaining training stability over weeks of GPU time, and making compute-optimal decisions worth millions of dollars. This lesson covers the key concepts: pre-training objectives, scaling laws, training recipes used by leading models, and the emerging Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture.
1. Pre-Training Objectives
1.1 Causal Language Modeling (CLM)
The standard GPT-style objective: predict the next token given all previous tokens.
Input:  [The] [cat] [sat] [on] [the]Target: [cat] [sat] [on] [the] [mat]Loss = -sum(log P(t_i | t_1, ..., t_{i-1})) / N
Used by: GPT family, Llama, Mistral, Falcon, Gemma
Advantages:
* Simple and scalable
* Natural fit for generation
* Can be trained on any text
1.2 Masked Language Modeling (MLM)
BERT-style: randomly mask 15% of tokens and predict them from context (both left and right):
Input:  [The] [cat] [MASK] [on] [the] [MASK]Target:             [sat]             [mat]Only compute loss on masked positions.
Used by: BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa
1.3 Prefix Language Modeling
A hybrid: the prefix (first part) uses bidirectional attention, and the rest uses causal attention:
Prefix (bidirectional):    [The] [cat] [sat]Causal continuation:       [on] [the] [mat]Prefix tokens can attend to each other.Continuation tokens can only attend to prefix + previous continuation tokens.
Used by: T5, PaLM (partially), UL2
1.4 Comparison
Objective | Direction | Generation | Understanding | Models
CLM | Left-to-right | Excellent | Good | GPT, Llama
MLM | Bidirectional | Poor | Excellent | BERT
Prefix LM | Both | Good | Good | T5, UL2
Key Insight: CLM has become the dominant pre-training objective for LLMs because it scales better and produces models that can both understand and generate text. The gap between CLM and MLM for understanding tasks has largely closed with scale — GPT-4 matches or exceeds BERT-style models on most NLU benchmarks.
2. Scaling Laws
2.1 Kaplan Scaling Laws (2020)
OpenAI's initial findings showed that test loss follows power-law relationships:
L(N) = (N_c / N)^alpha_N    (loss decreases with model size N)L(D) = (D_c / D)^alpha_D    (loss decreases with dataset size D)L(C) = (C_c / C)^alpha_C    (loss decreases with compute C)Where alpha_N ≈ 0.076, alpha_D ≈ 0.095, alpha_C ≈ 0.050
Key finding: For a fixed compute budget, it is better to train a larger model on less data than a smaller model on more data.
2.2 Chinchilla Scaling Laws (2022)
Hoffmann et al. at DeepMind revised these findings:
Optimal allocation for compute budget C:  N_opt ∝ C^0.5    (model parameters)  D_opt ∝ C^0.5    (training tokens)Rule of thumb: Tokens ≈ 20 * Parameters
Compute-Optimal Model | Parameters | Training Tokens
"Chinchilla" | 70B | 1.4T
Llama (over-trained) | 7B | 1T (143x ratio)
Llama 2 | 7B | 2T (286x ratio)
Llama 3 | 8B | 15T+ (1875x ratio)
Key Insight: Chinchilla showed that many existing LLMs (like GPT-3 175B trained on 300B tokens) were significantly undertrained. However, for inference efficiency, the trend has shifted toward over-training smaller models: Llama 3 8B was trained on 15T+ tokens, far beyond the Chinchilla-optimal ratio, because a smaller model that is cheaper to serve can match a larger model's quality if given enough training data.
2.3 Scaling Law Visualization
Loss ^     |     |\     | \     |  \     |   \  Large model, lots of data     |    \     |     \     |      \___________________________     |     |    Small model, lots of data     |  \     |   \___________     |     +-----------------------------------------> Compute (FLOPs)Key: Increasing model size gives steeper initial improvement,     but both need to be scaled together for efficiency.
3. Compute-Optimal Training
3.1 Estimating Compute
FLOPs for a transformer forward pass ≈ 2 * N * TWhere:  N = number of parameters  T = number of tokens in one passTotal training FLOPs ≈ 6 * N * DWhere:  D = total training tokens  Factor of 6: forward (2) + backward (4) per token
3.2 Compute Budget Planning
Given budget C (in GPU-hours):Available FLOPs = C * GPU_FLOPS * utilization  A100 (BF16): 312 TFLOPS * ~0.4 MFU = ~125 TFLOPS effective  H100 (BF16): 990 TFLOPS * ~0.4 MFU = ~396 TFLOPS effectiveExample: 1000 A100-hours  FLOPs = 1000 * 3600 * 125e12 = 4.5e20 FLOPs  Chinchilla-optimal: N ≈ 1.5B params, D ≈ 30B tokens
4. Data Mixing Strategies
4.1 Data Sources
Source | Quality | Diversity | Volume | Typical Weight
Web (Common Crawl) | Low-Medium | High | Trillions | 60-70%
Books | High | Medium | Billions | 5-10%
Wikipedia | High | Medium | Billions | 3-5%
Code (GitHub) | Medium | High | Billions | 5-15%
Academic papers | High | Low | Billions | 2-5%
Curated/Synthetic | Very High | Varies | Millions-Billions | 5-10%
4.2 Data Quality Pipeline
Raw Web Data (100+ TB)    |[URL Dedup] --> Remove duplicate URLs    |[Language ID] --> Filter to target languages    |[Quality Filter] --> Perplexity scoring, rule-based filters    |[Deduplication] --> MinHash LSH, exact substring dedup    |[PII Removal] --> Regex + NER for personal info    |[Content Filter] --> Toxicity, NSFW, harmful content    |[Mixing] --> Combine sources with target ratios    |Clean Training Data (~1-5 TB)
4.3 Curriculum Learning
Present data in a meaningful order:
# Example: Gradually increase data complexitycurriculum_schedule = {    0.0:  {'web': 0.4, 'wiki': 0.3, 'books': 0.2, 'code': 0.1},  # Easy first    0.3:  {'web': 0.5, 'wiki': 0.2, 'books': 0.15, 'code': 0.15},    0.7:  {'web': 0.6, 'wiki': 0.1, 'books': 0.1, 'code': 0.2},   # Harder later    0.9:  {'web': 0.5, 'wiki': 0.1, 'books': 0.1, 'code': 0.1, 'curated': 0.2},}
Note: Data quality is arguably more important than model architecture for LLM performance. The Llama team attributed much of their model's strength to careful data curation rather than architectural innovations.
5. Training Stability
5.1 Common Instabilities
Loss ^     |     |  Normal training                Loss spike     |   \                             /\     |    \                           /  \     |     \                         /    \     |      \                       /      \     |       \                     /        \___     |        \___________________/             \     |                                           \___     +---------------------------------------------> StepCauses of loss spikes:- Learning rate too high- Gradient explosion (numerical instability)- Bad data batches (corrupt or extremely long)- Attention entropy collapse
5.2 Prevention Strategies
Strategy | Description
Gradient clipping | Clip global norm to 1.0
QK LayerNorm | Normalize Q and K before attention
z-loss | Add small penalty on log(Z) to prevent log-sum-exp overflow
Data filtering | Remove samples with extreme loss
LR warmup | Critical for the first 0.1-1% of training
Checkpoint frequently | Save every 100-1000 steps
5.3 QK LayerNorm
Used in PaLM, Llama 3, and others:
class StableAttention(nn.Module):    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):        super().__init__()        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model)        self.q_norm = nn.LayerNorm(d_model // n_heads)        self.k_norm = nn.LayerNorm(d_model // n_heads)        # ... rest of attention
5.4 z-loss
Prevents logits from becoming too large:
def compute_z_loss(logits, z_loss_weight=1e-4):    """Penalize large logits for training stability."""    log_z = torch.logsumexp(logits, dim=-1)    z_loss = z_loss_weight * (log_z ** 2).mean()    return z_loss
6. The Llama / Mistral Training Recipe
6.1 Architecture Choices
Component | Llama 2 | Mistral 7B
Positional encoding | RoPE | RoPE
Normalization | RMSNorm (pre-norm) | RMSNorm (pre-norm)
Activation | SiLU/Swish | SiLU/Swish
Attention | GQA (Grouped Query) | GQA + Sliding Window
FFN | SwiGLU (2/3 expansion) | SwiGLU
Vocabulary | 32K (BPE) | 32K (BPE)
6.2 SwiGLU FFN
class SwiGLU(nn.Module):    """SwiGLU feed-forward: gate * swish(linear1(x)) * linear2(x)."""    def __init__(self, d_model, d_ff=None):        super().__init__()        d_ff = d_ff or int(2/3 * 4 * d_model)  # 2/3 of standard 4x expansion        # Round to nearest multiple of 256 for hardware efficiency        d_ff = 256 * ((d_ff + 255) // 256)        self.w1 = nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff, bias=False)  # Gate projection        self.w2 = nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model, bias=False)  # Down projection        self.w3 = nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff, bias=False)  # Up projection    def forward(self, x):        return self.w2(F.silu(self.w1(x)) * self.w3(x))
6.3 Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)
GQA uses fewer key-value heads than query heads, reducing memory during inference:
Multi-Head Attention (MHA): Q=32 heads, K=32 heads, V=32 headsGrouped-Query (GQA):        Q=32 heads, K=8 groups,  V=8 groupsMulti-Query (MQA):          Q=32 heads, K=1 head,    V=1 head4 query heads share each KV group:  Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4 --> K1, V1  Q5, Q6, Q7, Q8 --> K2, V2  ...
7. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)
7.1 Concept
MoE replaces the standard FFN with multiple "expert" FFNs and a gating network that routes each token to a subset of experts:
Input Token             |      [Gating Network]       / |    |    \      /  |    |     \Expert  Expert Expert Expert    (e.g., 8 experts)  1       2     3      4      \  |    |     /       \ |    |    /      Top-K selection (e.g., K=2)             |         [Weighted Sum]             |          Output
7.2 Gating Mechanism
class MoELayer(nn.Module):    """Mixture-of-Experts layer with top-k routing."""    def __init__(self, d_model, d_ff, num_experts=8, top_k=2):        super().__init__()        self.num_experts = num_experts        self.top_k = top_k        # Router        self.gate = nn.Linear(d_model, num_experts, bias=False)        # Experts        self.experts = nn.ModuleList([            SwiGLU(d_model, d_ff) for _ in range(num_experts)        ])    def forward(self, x):        B, T, D = x.shape        # Compute gating scores        gate_logits = self.gate(x)  # (B, T, num_experts)        gate_scores = F.softmax(gate_logits, dim=-1)        # Select top-k experts        top_k_scores, top_k_indices = torch.topk(gate_scores, self.top_k, dim=-1)        top_k_scores = top_k_scores / top_k_scores.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)  # Normalize        # Compute expert outputs (simplified; real impl uses sparse dispatch)        output = torch.zeros_like(x)        for i in range(self.top_k):            expert_idx = top_k_indices[:, :, i]  # (B, T)            for e in range(self.num_experts):                mask = (expert_idx == e)                if mask.any():                    expert_input = x[mask]                    expert_output = self.experts[e](expert_input)                    output[mask] += top_k_scores[:, :, i][mask].unsqueeze(-1) * expert_output        return output
7.3 Load Balancing
Without balancing, the router may send all tokens to a few experts:
def load_balancing_loss(gate_logits, num_experts, top_k=2):    """Auxiliary loss to encourage balanced expert usage."""    gate_probs = F.softmax(gate_logits, dim=-1)  # (B*T, num_experts)    # Fraction of tokens routed to each expert    tokens_per_expert = gate_probs.mean(dim=0)    # Ideal: uniform distribution = 1/num_experts    uniform = torch.ones_like(tokens_per_expert) / num_experts    # Load balancing loss (minimize deviation from uniform)    aux_loss = num_experts * (tokens_per_expert * uniform).sum()    return aux_loss
7.4 MoE Models
Model | Total Params | Active Params | Experts | Top-K
Mixtral 8x7B | 46.7B | 12.9B | 8 | 2
DeepSeek-MoE | 145B | 22B | 64 | 6
Grok-1 | 314B | ~86B | 8 | 2
Key Insight: MoE models achieve the quality of much larger dense models at a fraction of the inference cost. Mixtral 8x7B (47B total, 13B active) matches Llama 2 70B quality while being 6x cheaper to serve. The key challenge is training stability and ensuring balanced expert utilization.
8. Pre-Training Best Practices
8.1 Complete Training Configuration
training_config = {    # Architecture    'model_size': '7B',    'n_layers': 32,    'd_model': 4096,    'n_heads': 32,    'n_kv_heads': 8,        # GQA    'ffn_dim': 11008,       # SwiGLU with 2/3 expansion    'vocab_size': 32000,    'max_seq_len': 4096,    'norm': 'rmsnorm',    'activation': 'swiglu',    'pos_encoding': 'rope',    # Training    'total_tokens': 2_000_000_000_000,  # 2T tokens    'batch_size': 4_000_000,            # 4M tokens per batch    'micro_batch_size': 4,    'gradient_accumulation': 32,    'learning_rate': 3e-4,    'min_learning_rate': 3e-5,    'warmup_tokens': 2_000_000_000,     # 2B tokens warmup    'lr_schedule': 'cosine',    'weight_decay': 0.1,    'grad_clip': 1.0,    # Precision    'dtype': 'bfloat16',    # Parallelism    'tensor_parallel': 4,    'pipeline_parallel': 1,    'data_parallel': 'fsdp',  # Or ZeRO-3    # Stability    'qk_layernorm': True,    'z_loss_weight': 1e-4,    # Data    'data_mix': {        'web': 0.67,        'code': 0.12,        'books': 0.08,        'wikipedia': 0.05,        'academic': 0.04,        'curated': 0.04,    },}

Artificial Intelligence Research - Transfer Learning and Pre-trained Models
Lesson 01: Transfer Learning and Pre-trained Models
Introduction
Training a deep neural network from scratch requires vast amounts of data, compute, and time. Transfer learning sidesteps this cost by reusing knowledge that a model has already acquired on one task and applying it to a different — often related — task. It is arguably the single most impactful idea that made modern AI accessible to teams of all sizes.
Note: Transfer learning is not a single algorithm; it is a strategy. The specific implementation varies depending on the model architecture, the source task, and the target task.
1. What Is Transfer Learning?
At its core, transfer learning answers the question: "Can the representations learned by a model on Task A help solve Task B?"
1.1 Formal Definition
Given a source domain $D_S$ with learning task $T_S$ and a target domain $D_T$ with learning task $T_T$, transfer learning improves the learning of the target predictive function $f_T(\cdot)$ in $D_T$ using knowledge from $D_S$ and $T_S$, where $D_S \neq D_T$ or $T_S \neq T_T$.
1.2 Why It Works
Deep neural networks learn a hierarchy of features:
Layer 1-2:  Low-level features   (edges, textures, phonemes, subword tokens)Layer 3-5:  Mid-level features   (shapes, parts, phrases, syntactic patterns)Layer 6+:   High-level features  (objects, scenes, semantic meaning, reasoning)
The lower layers are general — they transfer well across tasks. The upper layers are task-specific — they usually need adaptation.
1.3 Transfer Learning Taxonomy
Transfer Learning├── Inductive Transfer Learning│   ├── Self-taught learning│   └── Multi-task learning├── Transductive Transfer Learning│   ├── Domain adaptation│   └── Sample selection bias└── Unsupervised Transfer Learning    ├── Self-supervised pre-training    └── Generative pre-training (GPT-style)
2. Feature Extraction vs. Fine-Tuning
These are the two primary strategies for applying transfer learning.
2.1 Feature Extraction
Use the pre-trained model as a fixed feature extractor. Freeze all layers, remove (or ignore) the final classification head, and train only a new head on top.
┌──────────────────────────────┐│  New Classification Head     │  ← Trainable├──────────────────────────────┤│  Pre-trained Backbone        │  ← FROZEN (weights do not update)│  (e.g., ResNet, BERT)        │└──────────────────────────────┘
When to use:
* Small target dataset (hundreds to low thousands of examples)
* Target task is similar to the source task
* Limited compute budget
2.2 Fine-Tuning
Unfreeze some or all layers of the pre-trained model and train them alongside the new head, typically with a smaller learning rate than training from scratch.
┌──────────────────────────────┐│  New Classification Head     │  ← Trainable (higher LR)├──────────────────────────────┤│  Upper Layers                │  ← Trainable (lower LR)├──────────────────────────────┤│  Lower Layers                │  ← Frozen or very low LR└──────────────────────────────┘
When to use:
* Moderate to large target dataset
* Target domain differs significantly from source domain
* You need maximum performance
2.3 Comparison Table
Aspect | Feature Extraction | Fine-Tuning
Trainable parameters | Few (head only) | Many (head + backbone)
Training time | Minutes | Hours
Data requirement | Low (100s of samples) | Medium-High (1K+)
Risk of overfitting | Low | Higher (mitigated with LR scheduling)
Performance ceiling | Lower | Higher
Compute cost | Low | Medium-High
Key Insight: A common pattern is to start with feature extraction, evaluate the baseline, then selectively unfreeze layers (top-down) to squeeze out extra performance — a technique called gradual unfreezing.
3. Domain Adaptation
Domain adaptation is a special case of transfer learning where the task remains the same but the data distribution changes.
3.1 Types of Domain Shift
Shift Type | Description | Example
Covariate shift | Input distribution changes | Medical images from different scanners
Prior probability shift | Label distribution changes | Fraud detection in different regions
Concept shift | Input-output mapping changes | Sentiment shifts over time
3.2 Domain Adaptation Techniques
* Discrepancy-based: Minimize the difference between source and target feature distributions (e.g., Maximum Mean Discrepancy — MMD).
* Adversarial-based: Use a domain discriminator to make learned features domain-invariant (e.g., Domain-Adversarial Neural Networks — DANN).
* Reconstruction-based: Use autoencoders to learn shared representations.
* Self-training / Pseudo-labeling: Use the source-trained model to label target data, then retrain.
Domain Adaptation with Adversarial Training============================================Source Data ──→ ┌────────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐                │  Feature        │────→│ Task          │ → Task LossTarget Data ──→ │  Extractor      │     │ Classifier    │                └───────┬────────┘     └──────────────┘                        │                        ▼                ┌────────────────┐                │  Domain         │ → Domain Loss (adversarial)                │  Discriminator  │                └────────────────┘
4. Model Hubs
Pre-trained models are shared through centralized repositories called model hubs. These dramatically lower the barrier to using transfer learning.
4.1 Hugging Face Hub
The largest open model hub, hosting 500K+ models across NLP, vision, audio, and multimodal tasks.
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer# Load any model with a single linetokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
Key features:
* Model cards with documentation
* Datasets library integration
* Spaces for demos
* Inference API
* Gated models (Llama, Gemma, etc.)
4.2 TensorFlow Hub
import tensorflow_hub as hub# Load a pre-trained image modelmodel = hub.KerasLayer("https://tfhub.dev/google/imagenet/mobilenet_v3_large_100_224/feature_vector/5")
4.3 PyTorch Hub
import torch# Load a model from PyTorch Hubmodel = torch.hub.load('pytorch/vision:v0.10.0', 'resnet50', pretrained=True)
4.4 ONNX Model Zoo
The Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) provides a framework-agnostic model format. ONNX Model Zoo hosts models in .onnx format that run on any ONNX-compatible runtime.
import onnxruntime as ortsession = ort.InferenceSession("model.onnx")outputs = session.run(None, {"input": input_data})
4.5 Hub Comparison
Hub | Frameworks | Model Count | Strengths
Hugging Face | PyTorch, TF, JAX, ONNX | 500K+ | Largest ecosystem, model cards, community
TF Hub | TensorFlow | 1K+ | Tight TF integration, SavedModel format
PyTorch Hub | PyTorch | 100s | Simple API, torch.hub.load()
ONNX Zoo | Framework-agnostic | 100s | Cross-framework deployment
5. Choosing the Right Pre-trained Model
Selecting the best starting checkpoint is critical. Here is a decision framework:
5.1 Decision Flowchart
What is your task?                          │          ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐          ▼               ▼               ▼       Text            Vision          Audio          │               │               │    ┌─────┴──────┐   ┌───┴────┐     ┌───┴────┐    ▼            ▼   ▼        ▼     ▼        ▼ Classify    Generate  Classify  Detect   ASR    TTS    │            │       │        │       │       │  BERT      GPT/Llama  ViT    YOLO   Whisper  Bark  RoBERTa   Mistral   ResNet  DETR   Wav2Vec  VITS  DeBERTa   Qwen      EfficientNet
5.2 Selection Criteria
* Task alignment: Was the model pre-trained on a similar task?
* Domain proximity: Does the pre-training data overlap with your target domain?
* Model size vs. budget: Larger models perform better but cost more.
* License: Check commercial use restrictions (e.g., Llama community license vs. Apache 2.0).
* Community support: More popular models have better tooling and debugging resources.
* Benchmark scores: Check leaderboards (Open LLM Leaderboard, Papers With Code).
Note: Bigger is not always better. A smaller model fine-tuned on domain-specific data often outperforms a larger general model on that domain.
6. Zero-Shot and Few-Shot Capabilities
Modern large pre-trained models can perform tasks they were never explicitly trained for.
6.1 Zero-Shot Learning
The model performs a task with no task-specific examples — relying entirely on its pre-training knowledge and natural language instructions.
from transformers import pipelineclassifier = pipeline("zero-shot-classification", model="facebook/bart-large-mnli")result = classifier(    "The new iPhone has an amazing camera system",    candidate_labels=["technology", "sports", "politics", "science"])# Output: technology (high confidence)
6.2 Few-Shot Learning (In-Context Learning)
Provide a small number of examples (shots) in the prompt. The model learns the pattern from these examples without any weight updates.
Classify the sentiment:Text: "This movie was fantastic!" → PositiveText: "Terrible waste of time." → NegativeText: "The acting was superb and the plot kept me engaged." → ???
6.3 Comparison
Method | Examples Needed | Weight Updates | Compute | Flexibility
Zero-shot | 0 | No | Minimal | High
Few-shot | 1-32 | No | Minimal | High
Fine-tuning | 100-100K+ | Yes | High | Task-specific
Key Insight: Zero/few-shot learning is best for prototyping and low-data scenarios. Once you have sufficient labeled data, fine-tuning almost always wins on accuracy.
7. Model Cards
A model card is a standardized document that accompanies a pre-trained model, providing essential information for responsible use.
7.1 Key Sections of a Model Card
Section | Contents
Model Details | Architecture, size, training data, framework
Intended Use | Primary use cases and out-of-scope uses
Training Data | Dataset description, size, preprocessing
Evaluation Results | Benchmarks, metrics, limitations
Ethical Considerations | Bias analysis, fairness, environmental impact
Limitations | Known failure modes, data gaps
7.2 Example Model Card (Abbreviated)
---model-index:- name: bert-base-uncased  results:  - task: { type: text-classification }    dataset: { name: GLUE, type: glue }    metrics:    - { name: Accuracy, type: accuracy, value: 79.6 }license: apache-2.0language: entags: [bert, fill-mask, transformers]---
Note: Always read the model card before using a pre-trained model. It tells you what the model can and cannot do, and highlights biases present in the training data.
8. Practical Transfer Learning Pipeline
Let's build a complete transfer learning pipeline step by step.
8.1 Pipeline Architecture
┌───────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌────────────────┐    ┌───────────┐│ Load       │───→│ Prepare      │───→│ Train/Fine-tune│───→│ Evaluate  ││ Pre-trained│    │ Dataset      │    │ (feature ext   │    │ & Export  ││ Model      │    │              │    │  or full FT)   │    │           │└───────────┘    └──────────────┘    └────────────────┘    └───────────┘
8.2 Code: Transfer Learning with Hugging Face
"""Transfer Learning Pipeline with Hugging Face Transformers=========================================================This script demonstrates both feature extraction and fine-tuningfor text classification using a pre-trained BERT model.Requirements:    pip install transformers datasets torch scikit-learn"""import torchimport numpy as npfrom datasets import load_datasetfrom transformers import (    AutoTokenizer,    AutoModelForSequenceClassification,    TrainingArguments,    Trainer,)from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score# ─────────────────────────────────────────────# 1. Configuration# ─────────────────────────────────────────────MODEL_NAME = "bert-base-uncased"       # Pre-trained checkpointDATASET_NAME = "imdb"                   # Target task datasetNUM_LABELS = 2                          # Binary sentimentMAX_LENGTH = 256                        # Max token lengthBATCH_SIZE = 16LEARNING_RATE = 2e-5                    # Small LR for fine-tuningNUM_EPOCHS = 3OUTPUT_DIR = "./transfer_learning_output"STRATEGY = "fine_tune"                  # "feature_extract" or "fine_tune"# ─────────────────────────────────────────────# 2. Load and Tokenize Dataset# ─────────────────────────────────────────────print("Loading dataset...")dataset = load_dataset(DATASET_NAME)tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_NAME)def tokenize_function(examples):    """Tokenize text inputs with padding and truncation."""    return tokenizer(        examples["text"],        padding="max_length",        truncation=True,        max_length=MAX_LENGTH,    )tokenized_datasets = dataset.map(tokenize_function, batched=True)# Use a smaller subset for demonstrationtrain_dataset = tokenized_datasets["train"].shuffle(seed=42).select(range(2000))eval_dataset = tokenized_datasets["test"].shuffle(seed=42).select(range(500))# ─────────────────────────────────────────────# 3. Load Pre-trained Model# ─────────────────────────────────────────────print(f"Loading pre-trained model: {MODEL_NAME}")model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(    MODEL_NAME,    num_labels=NUM_LABELS,)# ─────────────────────────────────────────────# 4. Apply Transfer Learning Strategy# ─────────────────────────────────────────────if STRATEGY == "feature_extract":    print("Strategy: Feature Extraction (freezing backbone)")    # Freeze all parameters in the base model    for param in model.bert.parameters():        param.requires_grad = False    # Only the classification head will be trained    trainable = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)    total = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())    print(f"Trainable parameters: {trainable:,} / {total:,} "          f"({100 * trainable / total:.2f}%)")elif STRATEGY == "fine_tune":    print("Strategy: Full Fine-Tuning")    trainable = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)    print(f"All {trainable:,} parameters are trainable")else:    raise ValueError(f"Unknown strategy: {STRATEGY}")# ─────────────────────────────────────────────# 5. Define Metrics# ─────────────────────────────────────────────def compute_metrics(eval_pred):    """Compute accuracy and F1 for evaluation."""    logits, labels = eval_pred    predictions = np.argmax(logits, axis=-1)    return {        "accuracy": accuracy_score(labels, predictions),        "f1": f1_score(labels, predictions, average="weighted"),    }# ─────────────────────────────────────────────# 6. Training Arguments# ─────────────────────────────────────────────training_args = TrainingArguments(    output_dir=OUTPUT_DIR,    num_train_epochs=NUM_EPOCHS,    per_device_train_batch_size=BATCH_SIZE,    per_device_eval_batch_size=BATCH_SIZE,    learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE,    weight_decay=0.01,    eval_strategy="epoch",    save_strategy="epoch",    load_best_model_at_end=True,    metric_for_best_model="accuracy",    logging_steps=50,    report_to="none",                   # Disable W&B / MLflow    fp16=torch.cuda.is_available(),     # Mixed precision if GPU)# ─────────────────────────────────────────────# 7. Create Trainer and Train# ─────────────────────────────────────────────trainer = Trainer(    model=model,    args=training_args,    train_dataset=train_dataset,    eval_dataset=eval_dataset,    compute_metrics=compute_metrics,)print("Starting training...")train_result = trainer.train()print(f"Training complete. Metrics: {train_result.metrics}")# ─────────────────────────────────────────────# 8. Evaluate# ─────────────────────────────────────────────eval_results = trainer.evaluate()print(f"\nEvaluation Results:")for key, value in eval_results.items():    print(f"  {key}: {value:.4f}")# ─────────────────────────────────────────────# 9. Save Model# ─────────────────────────────────────────────model_save_path = f"{OUTPUT_DIR}/best_model"trainer.save_model(model_save_path)tokenizer.save_pretrained(model_save_path)print(f"\nModel saved to {model_save_path}")# ─────────────────────────────────────────────# 10. Inference Example# ─────────────────────────────────────────────from transformers import pipelineclassifier = pipeline(    "sentiment-analysis",    model=model_save_path,    tokenizer=model_save_path,)test_texts = [    "This movie was absolutely brilliant! The acting was superb.",    "What a waste of time. The plot made no sense whatsoever.",    "It was okay, nothing special but not terrible either.",]print("\nInference Results:")for text in test_texts:    result = classifier(text)    print(f"  '{text[:50]}...' → {result[0]['label']} ({result[0]['score']:.3f})")
9. Advanced Transfer Learning Patterns
9.1 Gradual Unfreezing
Instead of fine-tuning all layers at once, unfreeze one layer group at a time, training for a few epochs between each unfreezing step.
# Gradual unfreezing schedulelayer_groups = [    model.bert.encoder.layer[10:],   # Unfreeze top 2 layers first    model.bert.encoder.layer[8:10],  # Then next 2    model.bert.encoder.layer[6:8],   # Continue...    model.bert.encoder.layer[:6],    # Finally the bottom layers]for i, group in enumerate(layer_groups):    print(f"Unfreezing group {i+1}/{len(layer_groups)}")    for layer in group:        for param in layer.parameters():            param.requires_grad = True    # Train for 1 epoch with this configuration    trainer.train()
9.2 Discriminative Learning Rates
Use different learning rates for different layers — lower LR for early layers, higher LR for later layers.
from torch.optim import AdamW# Group parameters with different learning ratesoptimizer_grouped_parameters = [    {"params": model.bert.embeddings.parameters(), "lr": 1e-6},    {"params": model.bert.encoder.layer[:6].parameters(), "lr": 5e-6},    {"params": model.bert.encoder.layer[6:].parameters(), "lr": 1e-5},    {"params": model.classifier.parameters(), "lr": 2e-5},]optimizer = AdamW(optimizer_grouped_parameters)
9.3 Cross-Lingual Transfer
Models like mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa learn multilingual representations. You can fine-tune on English data and the model transfers to other languages.
from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification# Fine-tune on English, evaluate on German, French, etc.model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(    "xlm-roberta-base",    num_labels=3,  # e.g., NLI: entailment, contradiction, neutral)
10. Common Pitfalls and Best Practices
10.1 Pitfalls
Pitfall | Symptom | Solution
Learning rate too high | Loss diverges or spikes | Use 1e-5 to 5e-5 for fine-tuning
Not enough data | Overfitting within 1 epoch | Use feature extraction or data augmentation
Domain mismatch | Low accuracy despite good training loss | Use domain-adaptive pre-training
Forgetting pre-trained knowledge | Performance drops mid-training | Use gradual unfreezing or lower LR
Wrong pre-trained model | Poor baseline | Match model pre-training to your domain
10.2 Best Practices
* Always establish a baseline — evaluate the pre-trained model zero-shot before any training.
* Start with feature extraction — if performance is acceptable, you are done.
* Use a learning rate finder — sweep LR from 1e-7 to 1e-3 and pick the steepest descent point.
* Monitor validation loss — stop training when it starts increasing (early stopping).
* Save checkpoints — you can always go back to the best checkpoint.
* Read the model card — understand what the model was trained on and its limitations.
Key Insight: Transfer learning is not magic. If the source and target domains are very different (e.g., transferring from English text to medical images), the benefit will be minimal. Always consider domain proximity.
11. Transfer Learning Across Modalities
11.1 Vision-Language Models
Models like CLIP, BLIP, and LLaVA bridge vision and language, enabling transfer across modalities.

11.2 Speech-to-Text Transfer
OpenAI Whisper was trained on 680K hours of multilingual audio. Fine-tuning it on a specific domain (medical dictation, legal transcription) is highly effective.
12. Summary
Concept | Key Takeaway
Transfer Learning | Reuse knowledge from one task to accelerate learning on another
Feature Extraction | Freeze backbone, train head only — fast and data-efficient
Fine-Tuning | Unfreeze layers, train end-to-end — higher performance ceiling
Domain Adaptation | Handle distribution shifts between source and target domains
Model Hubs | Centralized repositories for sharing pre-trained models
Zero/Few-Shot | Use large pre-trained models without any weight updates
Model Cards | Documentation that accompanies pre-trained models
