Artificial Intelligence Research - The Research Process in AI
Lesson 01: The Research Process in AI
Module 5: Advanced Research and Algorithm Improvement Course: AI Research Fundamentals
Introduction
Conducting research in artificial intelligence is fundamentally different from engineering work. Engineering solves known problems with established tools; research confronts problems where the solution — or even the precise problem statement — is unknown. This lesson demystifies the AI research process from the first spark of an idea to a published, reproducible contribution.
Understanding the research process is not just for academics. Practitioners who want to adapt, improve, or critically evaluate AI systems benefit enormously from knowing how ideas are born, tested, and validated. By the end of this lesson you will be able to identify open problems in the field, conduct a systematic literature review, design rigorous experiments, and understand the ethical obligations that come with publishing AI research.
1. Identifying Open Problems in AI
1.1 What Makes a Problem "Open"?
An open problem is one for which no satisfactory solution currently exists. In AI, this is nuanced: a problem may have partial solutions that fail under distribution shift, scale poorly, lack theoretical guarantees, or perform well on benchmarks but not in deployment.
Open problems typically fall into one of four categories:
Category | Description | Example
Unsolved | No adequate solution exists | General-purpose robotic manipulation
Partially solved | Solutions exist but with significant limitations | Long-context reasoning in LLMs
Solved but not understood | Works empirically, mechanism unknown | Why transformers generalize so well
Solved but not practical | Theoretically valid, too expensive | Exact Bayesian inference at scale
1.2 Sources of Open Problems
Reading survey papers and benchmarks. NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, and ACL publish annual outstanding papers lists. Benchmark leaderboards (SuperGLUE, BIG-Bench, HELM) reveal what systems still cannot do well.
Watching error analysis sections. The most honest part of any paper is its "limitations" or "failure modes" section. These are direct invitations for follow-up research.
Talking to practitioners. Industry practitioners deal with problems that academics have not yet formalized. Deployment challenges — latency, calibration, fairness under covariate shift — often become tomorrow's research topics.
Following workshop proceedings. Workshops at major conferences explicitly host speculative, unfinished work. ICML "Workshop on Challenges in Deployable Generative AI" or NeurIPS "ML Safety Workshop" are examples.
1.3 Techniques for Problem Discovery
Negative results mining. Search for papers whose titles include "failure," "limitations," "when X fails," or "pitfalls." These map the boundary of current capability.
Ablation archaeology. Read ablation tables in published papers. When an ablation shows that removing component X barely affects performance, that component's role is an open question.
Crossing domain boundaries. Many breakthroughs come from applying ideas from one domain to another. Attention mechanisms (originally from NLP) revolutionized computer vision via ViT (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020).
Key Concept: The Streetlight Effect Researchers, like everyone, tend to look where the light is — in AI, where good benchmarks and compute are available. Actively seeking problems in poorly benchmarked or resource-constrained domains often yields high-impact, low-competition research.
2. The Literature Review Process
2.1 Why Literature Reviews Matter
A literature review serves three purposes: it prevents re-inventing the wheel, it situates your contribution relative to existing work, and it identifies methodological precedents you can build on. Skipping or rushing this step is the most common cause of rejected papers.
2.2 Structured Search Strategy
A systematic literature review follows a defined protocol:
* Define scope: What question are you investigating? What time period? What venues?
* Generate search terms: Use controlled vocabularies (ACM Computing Classification System) and free-text keywords.
* Select databases: Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, arXiv, Papers With Code.
* Screen results: Title/abstract screening first, then full-text.
* Snowball: Follow citations forward (who cited this?) and backward (what did this cite?).
* Synthesize: Organize findings by theme, not chronology.
2.3 Reading Order and Depth
Not all papers deserve equal time. Use a tiered approach:
* Tier 1 — Skim (5 min): Title, abstract, conclusion, figures. Is it relevant?
* Tier 2 — Survey (20 min): Introduction, section headings, key tables. What does it claim and how does it measure success?
* Tier 3 — Deep read (2+ hours): Full paper with derivations verified. For the 5–10 most relevant papers.
2.4 Tools for Literature Management
# Install Zotero CLI companion (optional)pip install pyzotero# Papers With Code API exampleimport requestsresponse = requests.get(    "https://paperswithcode.com/api/v1/papers/",    params={"q": "reinforcement learning from human feedback", "items_per_page": 10})papers = response.json()["results"]for p in papers:    print(p["title"], p["arxiv_id"])
Use Zotero or Mendeley for reference management. Tag papers with themes (e.g., #reward-modeling, #alignment, #scalability) rather than keeping flat lists.
2.5 Identifying the State of the Art
"State of the art" (SOTA) is a moving target. Use Papers With Code's task pages to find current benchmark leaders. Always check the date — a SOTA result from 2022 may be obsolete.
Key Concept: Related Work vs. Background "Background" covers foundational concepts your reader needs. "Related work" positions your contribution against existing approaches. Conflating these sections leads to papers that explain things the community already knows while failing to justify novelty.
3. Formulating Research Questions
3.1 Criteria for a Good Research Question
A well-formed research question in AI satisfies FINER criteria:
* Feasible: Can be answered with available compute, data, and time.
* Interesting: The answer would matter to the community.
* Novel: Not already answered in the literature.
* Ethical: Does not require harmful data collection or deployment.
* Relevant: Connects to a meaningful scientific or practical problem.
3.2 Sharpening Vague Ideas
Research questions evolve from vague intuitions to precise hypotheses. Consider this progression:
Stage | Statement
Vague idea | "Transformers might be worse at reasoning than we think"
Research direction | "Transformer performance on symbolic reasoning benchmarks may overfit to surface patterns"
Testable hypothesis | "A transformer trained on GSM8K achieves near-zero accuracy on isomorphic problems with permuted variable names, indicating reliance on lexical shortcuts rather than reasoning"
The third formulation specifies a model class, a dataset, an evaluation protocol, and an expected outcome — all falsifiable.
3.3 Types of Research Contributions
Not every paper proposes a new algorithm. Contributions can be:
* New method: A novel algorithm or architecture (e.g., attention mechanism, LoRA)
* New analysis: Theoretical or empirical insight into existing methods (e.g., "Grokking" paper by Power et al., 2022)
* New dataset/benchmark: Resources that enable future research (e.g., BIG-Bench)
* Negative result: Demonstrating that a believed approach fails under certain conditions
* Replication/survey: Systematic evaluation or reproduction of prior claims
4. Experimental Design
4.1 Principles of Experimental Design
Good experimental design in ML research borrows from classical statistics but has field-specific considerations.
Control variables. Change one thing at a time. If you compare optimizer A to optimizer B while also changing the learning rate schedule, you cannot attribute performance differences to the optimizer.
Baselines. Always include: (1) a naive baseline (random, majority class), (2) the previous SOTA, and (3) an ablated version of your own method.
Statistical significance. Single-run results are unreliable. Report mean and standard deviation across at least 3–5 seeds.
import numpy as npfrom scipy import stats# Results from 5 independent runsmethod_a = np.array([82.1, 81.9, 83.0, 82.5, 82.3])method_b = np.array([80.1, 80.5, 79.8, 80.9, 80.3])t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_ind(method_a, method_b)print(f"Method A: {method_a.mean():.2f} ± {method_a.std():.2f}")print(f"Method B: {method_b.mean():.2f} ± {method_b.std():.2f}")print(f"t-statistic: {t_stat:.3f}, p-value: {p_value:.4f}")# p < 0.05 suggests statistically significant difference
4.2 Ablation Studies
Ablation studies systematically remove or alter components of your method to understand each component's contribution. A rigorous ablation table looks like:
Model Variant | Accuracy | Notes
Full model | 84.2 | All components
w/o component A | 81.1 | -3.1 points
w/o component B | 82.9 | -1.3 points
w/o A and B | 79.3 | -4.9 points
Baseline | 78.0 | Prior SOTA
4.3 Hyperparameter Sensitivity
Report how sensitive your method is to hyperparameter choices. A method that achieves SOTA only at exactly one learning rate is not practically useful.
import matplotlib.pyplot as pltlearning_rates = [1e-5, 5e-5, 1e-4, 5e-4, 1e-3]performance   = [78.1, 82.3, 84.2, 83.1, 79.5]plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))plt.plot(learning_rates, performance, marker='o')plt.xscale('log')plt.xlabel('Learning Rate')plt.ylabel('Validation Accuracy (%)')plt.title('Performance vs. Learning Rate')plt.grid(True)plt.savefig('lr_sensitivity.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
4.4 Train/Validation/Test Splits
A critical and frequently violated principle: the test set must never influence any decision. This includes hyperparameter tuning. Use a held-out test set only for final evaluation, and report results only once.
5. Reproducibility in AI Research
5.1 The Reproducibility Crisis
A 2019 study by Pineau et al. found that fewer than 15% of AI papers at major venues provided enough information to reproduce their results. This "reproducibility crisis" undermines scientific progress and erodes trust in reported results.
5.2 Making Your Work Reproducible
Code release. Release code with every paper. Use GitHub and archive with Zenodo for a permanent DOI.
Environment specification. Pin all dependencies:
# requirements.txttorch==2.1.0transformers==4.36.0numpy==1.26.0scipy==1.11.4# Or use conda:conda env export > environment.yml
Seed management. Set all random seeds explicitly:
import random, numpy as np, torchdef set_seed(seed: int = 42):    random.seed(seed)    np.random.seed(seed)    torch.manual_seed(seed)    torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)    # For full determinism (slower):    torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True    torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False
Model checkpoints. Release trained model weights when feasible (Hugging Face Model Hub is the standard for NLP/CV).
Experiment tracking. Use Weights & Biases, MLflow, or similar tools to log every experiment automatically:
import wandbwandb.init(project="my-research", config={    "learning_rate": 1e-4,    "batch_size": 32,    "architecture": "transformer-base",    "seed": 42,})# During training:wandb.log({"train_loss": loss.item(), "val_acc": val_acc, "epoch": epoch})
5.3 The ML Reproducibility Checklist
The NeurIPS Reproducibility Checklist (Pineau et al., 2021) asks authors to confirm:
* All training details (optimizer, lr schedule, regularization) are reported
* Model size (parameters) and computational budget (GPU-hours) are stated
* Dataset splits and preprocessing steps are described
* Evaluation metrics and how they are computed are defined
* Results include error bars from multiple runs
* Code is publicly available
Key Concept: Compute Transparency Reporting GPU-hours spent is increasingly expected. A method that achieves +1% accuracy but requires 10x more compute may not be a practical advance. Carbon footprint reporting is an emerging norm (see Strubell et al., 2019, "Energy and Policy Considerations for Deep Learning in NLP").
6. Research Ethics in AI
6.1 Data Ethics
Consent and provenance. Data used for training must have clear provenance. Common Crawl and other web-scraped datasets may contain personally identifiable information (PII), copyrighted material, or harmful content.
Representation and bias. Training data that underrepresents demographic groups leads to systems that perform worse for those groups. Document dataset composition and measure performance disaggregated by subgroup.
Privacy. Models can memorize training data. Large language models have been shown to reproduce verbatim text from training corpora, including private information (Carlini et al., 2021, "Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models").
6.2 Dual-Use and Harm Potential
Some AI capabilities can be weaponized: text generation for disinformation, image synthesis for non-consensual content, code generation for malware. Researchers must consider:
* What is the realistic harm vector of my research?
* Does the benefit to legitimate users outweigh the risk of misuse?
* Should certain capabilities or datasets be kept confidential?
6.3 Authorship and Credit
Ghost authorship (listing someone who did not contribute) and gift authorship (excluding someone who did contribute) are both unethical. The CRediT taxonomy (Contributor Roles Taxonomy) provides a structured way to attribute contributions:
* Conceptualization, Methodology, Software, Validation
* Formal analysis, Investigation, Data curation
* Writing (original draft), Writing (review & editing)
* Visualization, Supervision, Project administration, Funding acquisition
6.4 Conflicts of Interest and Transparency
Disclose funding sources and conflicts of interest. Corporate-funded research is not inherently biased, but readers deserve to evaluate it in context.
7. arXiv and Conference Workflows
7.1 The arXiv Preprint Server
arXiv.org is the primary preprint server for AI research. Uploading to arXiv before peer review has become standard practice. Benefits:
* Establishes priority (timestamp your idea)
* Enables community feedback before formal review
* Accelerates knowledge dissemination (peer review takes 3–12 months)
Submission process:
* Prepare PDF and source files (LaTeX)
* Choose category: cs.LG (Machine Learning), cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.CV, stat.ML
* Submit; moderation takes 1–2 business days
* Paper receives an arXiv ID (e.g., arXiv:2301.12345)
7.2 Major AI Venues and Their Timelines
Venue | Type | Typical Deadline | Notification | Notes
NeurIPS | Conference | May | Sep | Double-blind
ICML | Conference | Jan | May | Double-blind
ICLR | Conference | Oct | Jan | Open review (OpenReview.net)
ACL/EMNLP/NAACL | Conference | Feb/Jun | May/Sep | NLP-focused
CVPR/ICCV/ECCV | Conference | Nov/Mar | Mar/Jun | Vision-focused
JMLR | Journal | Rolling | Rolling | Open access
TMLR | Journal | Rolling | Rolling | Reproducibility focus
7.3 The Conference Submission Pipeline
[Research] → [Draft] → [Internal Review] → [arXiv Upload]     ↓[Submission to Conference]     ↓[Desk Rejection? → Revise or Resubmit elsewhere]     ↓[Peer Review (2–4 reviewers, 4–8 weeks)]     ↓[Author Response / Rebuttal (1–2 weeks)]     ↓[Decision: Accept / Reject / Revise]     ↓[Camera-ready Preparation]     ↓[Presentation at Conference]
7.4 OpenReview and Transparency
ICLR uses OpenReview, making all reviews, author responses, and reviewer discussions public. This is a valuable resource for learning how papers are evaluated. Reading rejected papers and their reviews is highly educational.

Next Lesson: Lesson 02 — Reading and Writing AI Papers
Artificial Intelligence Research - Reading and Writing AI Papers
Lesson 02: Reading and Writing AI Papers
Module 5: Advanced Research and Algorithm Improvement Course: AI Research Fundamentals
Introduction
Reading and writing research papers are distinct skills that most practitioners never formally learn. Papers are not meant to be read front-to-back like textbooks; they are dense, nonlinear documents written for expert audiences under tight page limits. Similarly, writing a paper is not merely describing your experiments — it is constructing an argument that convinces skeptical reviewers your contribution is real, significant, and correctly measured.
This lesson equips you to read any AI paper efficiently and extract its core claims, and to write papers that communicate clearly and withstand rigorous peer review. We also cover the LaTeX typesetting system used universally in AI research and the mechanics of the submission and review process.
1. How to Read AI Papers Efficiently
1.1 The Three-Pass Method
Keshav's three-pass method (2007) is the standard framework for reading research papers. Rather than reading linearly, it reads the paper at increasing levels of detail over three distinct passes.
Pass 1 — The Bird's Eye View (5–10 minutes)
Goal: Decide if the paper is worth reading further.
* Read the title and abstract carefully.
* Read the introduction's first and last paragraphs.
* Read all section headings to understand the structure.
* Glance at all figures and tables — especially the main results table.
* Read the conclusion.
After Pass 1, you should be able to answer:
* What category of paper is this (algorithm, analysis, dataset, survey)?
* What problem does it claim to solve?
* What is the claimed main result?
Pass 2 — The Content Pass (1 hour)
Goal: Understand the paper's substance without getting lost in proofs.
* Read the paper with attention, but skip proofs and detailed derivations.
* Note every claim the authors make and identify the evidence supporting it.
* Examine figures and tables critically — can you reproduce them mentally?
* Mark anything you do not understand without stopping to resolve it.
* Note references you should follow up on.
After Pass 2, you should be able to summarize the paper to someone else.
Pass 3 — The Deep Dive (4+ hours for key papers)
Goal: Virtual re-implementation — understand every detail.
* Verify all mathematical derivations independently.
* Identify every assumption the authors make.
* Challenge the experimental design: are baselines fair? Are ablations comprehensive?
* Think about alternative explanations for the reported results.
* Consider failure modes not tested in the paper.
1.2 Reading the Abstract
The abstract follows a predictable structure. Learning to decode it instantly saves time:
Sentence 1–2: Context / motivation (What problem exists?)Sentence 3:   Gap / limitation of prior work (Why hasn't it been solved?)Sentence 4:   "In this paper, we..." (What did you do?)Sentence 5–6: Method summary (How?)Sentence 7–8: Key results (How well does it work?)Sentence 9:   Implications / broader significance
Example decoding — from "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017):
Sentence | Function
"The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks..." | Context
"...that include an encoder and a decoder." | Context continued
"The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism." | Prior work
"We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer..." | Contribution
"...based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely." | Method summary
"Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality..." | Results
"...while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train." | Secondary results
1.3 Evaluating the Contributions Section
Most papers explicitly list contributions, usually as bullet points in the introduction. Read these skeptically:
* Are the contributions specific or vague ("we propose a new method")?
* Do the contributions match the experiments that follow?
* Are claims quantified ("achieves 3.2 BLEU improvement") or qualitative?
* Is any contribution already present in prior work (a common reviewer complaint)?
1.4 Critically Reading the Experiments Section
The experiments section is where papers can most easily mislead. Check for:
Cherry-picking. Are results reported only on benchmarks where the method works? A new NLP method that is only evaluated on one dataset is suspicious.
Unfair baselines. Is the proposed method compared to the strongest available baselines? Is the baseline given the same hyperparameter tuning budget as the proposed method?
Missing ablations. If the method has 5 novel components, are ablations provided for each?
Statistical significance. Are error bars reported? With n=1 run, even a 5-point accuracy gap could be noise.
Metric choice. Does the reported metric align with the stated goal? A model that maximizes BLEU may not produce more human-like translations.
Key Concept: Goodhart's Law in Benchmarks "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." AI systems are increasingly optimized for specific benchmarks through dataset contamination, prompt engineering, or task-specific tuning. High benchmark performance does not always generalize to real-world capability.
2. Anatomy of an AI Research Paper
2.1 Standard Paper Structure
A typical AI conference paper (8–9 pages, double-column) follows this structure:
TitleAuthors and AffiliationsAbstract (250 words)1. Introduction         (1–1.5 pages)2. Related Work         (0.5–1 page)3. Method               (2–3 pages)4. Experiments          (2–3 pages)   4.1 Setup   4.2 Main Results   4.3 Ablation Studies   4.4 Analysis5. Conclusion           (0.5 page)References              (1–1.5 pages)Appendix (optional, unlimited pages in most venues)
2.2 What Each Section Must Accomplish
Introduction:
* Hook the reader with the problem's importance
* Describe the gap in current solutions
* State your contribution clearly (often as bullets)
* Provide a roadmap of the paper
Related Work:
* Group prior work thematically (not chronologically)
* Distinguish your work from each group
* Be generous — a reviewer who worked on something similar will notice if you missed it
Method:
* Be precise enough that a competent researcher can re-implement
* Use notation consistently (define all symbols)
* Explain the intuition before the formalism
* Include an architecture figure or algorithm box
Experiments:
* State your experimental hypotheses before results
* Describe datasets, metrics, and implementation details in sufficient detail
* Present results with statistical context
Conclusion:
* Summarize contributions (do not introduce new ideas)
* Acknowledge limitations honestly
* Suggest concrete future work directions
3. Writing Structure and Style
3.1 The Rhetorical Arc of a Research Paper
Think of a paper as a legal argument, not a story. You are convincing a skeptical judge (reviewer) that:
* The problem is real and important
* Existing solutions are insufficient
* Your approach is sound and novel
* Your experiments prove it works
* The community should care
Every section supports this argument. Material that does not support the argument should be cut.
3.2 Writing the Introduction
The introduction follows the IMRAD-hook structure:
Hook:       One compelling sentence that makes the reader careProblem:    What is hard and why does it matter?Gap:        What is missing from current solutions?Insight:    What is the key idea that enables your solution?Approach:   How does your method implement this insight?Results:    What did you demonstrate?Roadmap:    "The rest of this paper is organized as follows..."
Example of a weak vs. strong opening sentence:
* Weak: "Deep learning has achieved great success in many tasks."
* Strong: "Despite superhuman performance on chess and Go, state-of-the-art AI systems fail catastrophically when evaluated on games with slightly modified rules — a brittleness that calls into question the nature of the 'understanding' these systems acquire."
3.3 Writing Related Work
A common mistake is writing related work as an annotated bibliography: "Smith et al. (2019) proposed X. Jones et al. (2020) proposed Y." This tells the reader what exists but not why your work is different.
Instead, organize by research theme and contrast each group with your work:
## Related Work**Efficient Transformers.** A line of work reduces the O(n²) attention complexity through sparse attention (Child et al., 2019), linear approximations (Katharopoulos et al., 2020), and locality constraints (Beltagy et al., 2020). Unlike these methods, which require modifying the attention pattern, our approach operates on the embedding space and is compatible with any attention implementation.
3.4 Writing the Method Section
Use the following structure:
* Problem formulation: Define notation and the formal problem
* Intuition: Explain the core idea in plain language with a motivating example
* Algorithm: Give the full formal description
* Implementation details: Hyperparameters, architecture choices, training procedure
For clarity, use algorithm boxes:
Algorithm 1: Proposed Training Procedure─────────────────────────────────────────Input: Dataset D, model f_θ, learning rate ηOutput: Trained parameters θ*1: Initialize θ randomly2: for epoch = 1 to E do3:     for batch (x, y) in D do4:         ℓ ← L(f_θ(x), y) + λ · R(θ)5:         θ ← θ − η · ∇_θ ℓ6:     end for7:     Evaluate on validation set8: end for9: return θ* ← argmax_{θ} val_acc
3.5 Writing the Experiments Section
Lead with experimental hypotheses, not results. For each experiment, state what question it answers:
To evaluate whether our method generalizes across domains (RQ2), we compare against all baselines on five datasets spanning three domains: newswire, scientific literature, and social media.
Then present results, then interpret them.
3.6 Common Writing Pitfalls
Pitfall | Example | Fix
Weasel words | "significantly better" | "3.2 BLEU higher (p < 0.01)"
Passive overuse | "it was observed that" | "We observe that"
Undefined acronyms | "using RLHF with PPO" | Define at first use
Overclaiming | "solves the alignment problem" | "improves alignment on our benchmark"
Burying the lede | Results appear only in section 4 | State key results in abstract and intro

5. The Submission Process
5.1 Preparing a Submission
Before submitting, check every item on this list:
Content checklist:
* Abstract matches the actual content of the paper
* All claims are supported by evidence in the paper
* Limitations section is included and honest
* Broader impact / ethics statement (required by most venues)
* All figures have captions and are referenced in the text
* All tables have captions and are referenced in the text
* Page limit is respected (check conference guidelines)
Technical checklist:
* PDF compiles without errors or warnings
* Anonymous version prepared for double-blind review (remove author names, affiliations, acknowledgments, links to non-anonymous code)
* Supplementary material properly formatted
* arXiv ID excluded from blind submission (if required)
5.2 Anonymization for Double-Blind Review
Most venues require double-blind review. Common mistakes in anonymization:
% BAD: Revealing identity through self-citationOur method builds on our prior work [Smith et al., 2022].% FIX: Use third person for own workOur method builds on Smith et al. [2022].% BAD: Linking to non-anonymous resourcesCode available at github.com/myname/myproject% FIX: Use anonymous linkCode available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/...
5.3 Supplementary Material
Supplementary (or appendix) sections should contain:
* Additional experiments that support claims but do not fit in the main paper
* Full proofs of theoretical results stated in the main paper
* Extended ablations and sensitivity analyses
* Dataset details (collection methodology, statistics, sample examples)
* Implementation details (full hyperparameter tables, architecture specs)
* Broader impact statement (if required separately)
6. Peer Review
6.1 How Peer Review Works in AI
AI conference review typically follows this process:
* Submission — Authors submit to a portal (OpenReview, CMT, SoftConf)
* Area Chair assignment — An area chair (AC) oversees 10–20 papers
* Reviewer assignment — 3–4 reviewers assigned per paper
* Review period — Reviewers read and write reviews (3–6 weeks)
* Rebuttal period — Authors respond to reviews (1–2 weeks)
* Discussion — Reviewers discuss among themselves, possibly updating scores
* Meta-review — AC writes a summary recommendation
* Decision — Program chairs make final accept/reject decisions
6.2 Understanding Reviewer Scores
At NeurIPS and ICLR, reviewers typically score papers on:
* Soundness/Correctness (1–4): Is the work technically correct?
* Contribution/Novelty (1–4): Is the contribution significant and new?
* Presentation (1–4): Is the paper clearly written?
* Overall recommendation (1–10 at ICLR; Reject/Weak Reject/Weak Accept/Accept at NeurIPS)
An "8" at ICLR (strong accept) means the paper is likely to be a top-10% paper. A "5" or "6" (weak accept) requires convincing rebuttal or discussion.
6.3 Writing a Rebuttal
The rebuttal is your chance to address reviewer concerns. It is not a place to submit new experiments (usually), but to clarify misunderstandings and point to evidence already in the paper.
Rebuttal structure:
We thank all reviewers for their thoughtful comments. We address each concern below.**R1, R3: Comparison with [Missing Baseline]**We agree this is an important baseline. In Appendix B (Table 8), we include this comparison — our method outperforms it by 2.1 points on the main metric. We will make this result more prominent in the revised paper.**R2: Statistical significance**Reviewer 2 notes our results lack error bars. We ran all experiments with 5 random seeds; the standard deviations are ≤ 0.3% for all reported numbers (Table 1). We will add this information to the camera-ready version.**R3: Scalability concerns**The reviewer questions how our method scales to longer sequences. Figure 4 (right) shows scaling behavior up to 4096 tokens; our method's complexity is O(n log n) vs. O(n²) for the baseline, making it more favorable at longer lengths.
Rebuttal dos and don'ts:
Do | Don't
Be respectful and professional | Be defensive or dismissive
Address every reviewer concern | Ignore critical concerns
Point to existing evidence | Promise future experiments
Acknowledge legitimate weaknesses | Argue with reviewer's judgment
Be concise (500–1000 words) | Write an essay
7. After Acceptance: Camera-Ready and Beyond
7.1 Camera-Ready Preparation
After acceptance, you have typically 1–2 weeks to prepare the final version. This is your last chance to:
* Fix all typos and grammatical errors
* Add acknowledgments and grant numbers
* Deanonymize (add author names and affiliations)
* Update the paper based on reviewer feedback (within page limits)
* Add a link to your public code repository
7.2 Presenting Your Work
Poster presentations. AI conferences are predominantly poster-based. An effective poster:
* States the problem and result in the title area (readable from 3m)
* Uses figures as the primary communication medium
* Has minimal text (bullets, not paragraphs)
* Includes a QR code linking to the paper and code
Oral presentations (5–10% of accepted papers at top venues):
* 15-minute talk + 5 minutes Q&A (typical)
* First 3 minutes: motivate the problem for non-experts
* Middle 8 minutes: method and key results
* Last 2 minutes: broader impact and future work
* Prepare for adversarial questions
7.3 Building a Research Portfolio
Each paper is a data point in a research identity. Over time, aim for:
* A clear research theme (not scattered across disconnected topics)
* Impact beyond metrics (code used by others, cited in follow-up work)
* Service to the community (reviewing for conferences, organizing workshops)
* Mentorship (working with junior researchers)

Next Lesson: Lesson 03 — Reinforcement Learning Foundations
Artificial Intelligence Research - Reinforcement Learning Foundations
Lesson 03: Reinforcement Learning Foundations
Module 5: Advanced Research and Algorithm Improvement Course: AI Research Fundamentals
Introduction
Reinforcement learning (RL) is the study of how an agent can learn to make sequences of decisions by interacting with an environment and receiving feedback in the form of rewards. Unlike supervised learning, there is no labeled dataset; the agent must discover which actions lead to good outcomes through trial and error.
RL is the algorithmic backbone of some of the most striking AI achievements: AlphaGo defeating world champions at Go, robots learning to walk from scratch, and — most relevant to this course — fine-tuning large language models to be helpful, harmless, and honest (Lesson 04). Understanding RL at a mathematical level is essential for working with any of these systems.
This lesson progresses from the foundational mathematical framework (MDPs) through classical algorithms (Q-learning) to modern policy gradient methods (PPO), with working code examples throughout using the Gymnasium library.
1. Markov Decision Processes (MDPs)
1.1 The Formal Framework
An MDP is defined by the tuple $(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, \mathcal{P}, \mathcal{R}, \gamma)$:
* $\mathcal{S}$ — State space: the set of all possible situations the agent can be in
* $\mathcal{A}$ — Action space: the set of all actions the agent can take
* $\mathcal{P}(s' \mid s, a)$ — Transition function: probability of reaching state $s'$ from state $s$ after taking action $a$
* $\mathcal{R}(s, a, s')$ — Reward function: immediate reward received after transitioning
* $\gamma \in [0, 1)$ — Discount factor: how much future rewards are weighted relative to immediate rewards
The Markov property is the key assumption: the next state depends only on the current state and action, not on history. Formally:
$$P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t, s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, \ldots) = P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t)$$
1.2 The Agent-Environment Interaction Loop
┌─────────────────────┐         │      Environment    │         │                     │    ┌────┤  s_{t+1}, r_t       │◄──── a_t ────┐    │    │                     │               │    │    └─────────────────────┘               │    │                                          │    └──► s_t ────► Agent ───────────────────────┘
At each timestep $t$:
* Agent observes state $s_t$
* Agent selects action $a_t \sim \pi(\cdot \mid s_t)$
* Environment transitions to $s_{t+1} \sim \mathcal{P}(\cdot \mid s_t, a_t)$
* Agent receives reward $r_t = \mathcal{R}(s_t, a_t, s_{t+1})$
1.3 Returns and Discounting
The return $G_t$ is the total discounted reward from timestep $t$:
$$G_t = r_t + \gamma r_{t+1} + \gamma^2 r_{t+2} + \cdots = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k r_{t+k}$$
The discount factor $\gamma$ serves two purposes:
* Mathematical: ensures $G_t$ is finite for infinite-horizon problems
* Economic: captures the preference for immediate rewards over delayed ones
When $\gamma = 0$, the agent is myopic (only cares about immediate reward). When $\gamma \to 1$, the agent is far-sighted.
Key Concept: Episodic vs. Continuing Tasks Episodic tasks have a natural endpoint (e.g., a game of chess). Continuing tasks run indefinitely (e.g., a thermostat). For episodic tasks, the return is a finite sum; for continuing tasks, discounting is required to keep returns finite.
2. Policy and Value Functions
2.1 The Policy
A policy $\pi$ defines the agent's behavior — a mapping from states to action probabilities:
$$\pi(a \mid s) = P(A_t = a \mid S_t = s)$$
A deterministic policy maps each state to a single action: $\pi(s) = a$. A stochastic policy assigns probabilities over actions — essential for exploration.
2.2 The State-Value Function
The state-value function $V^\pi(s)$ is the expected return when starting in state $s$ and following policy $\pi$ thereafter:
$$V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}\pi \left[ G_t \mid S_t = s \right] = \mathbb{E}\pi \left[ \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k r_{t+k} \mid S_t = s \right]$$
2.3 The Action-Value (Q) Function
The action-value function $Q^\pi(s, a)$ is the expected return when starting in state $s$, taking action $a$, and then following policy $\pi$:
$$Q^\pi(s, a) = \mathbb{E}_\pi \left[ G_t \mid S_t = s, A_t = a \right]$$
The relationship between $V$ and $Q$:
$$V^\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s) Q^\pi(s, a)$$
2.4 The Optimal Policy
The optimal value function $V^(s) = \max_\pi V^\pi(s)$ and $Q^(s,a) = \max_\pi Q^\pi(s,a)$.
The optimal policy is then:
$$\pi^(s) = \arg\max_a Q^(s, a)$$
Any policy that acts greedily with respect to $Q^*$ is an optimal policy.
3. Bellman Equations
3.1 Bellman Expectation Equations
The Bellman equations express the recursive relationship between value functions. For $V^\pi$:
$$V^\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s) \sum_{s'} \mathcal{P}(s' \mid s, a) \left[ \mathcal{R}(s, a, s') + \gamma V^\pi(s') \right]$$
For $Q^\pi$:
$$Q^\pi(s, a) = \sum_{s'} \mathcal{P}(s' \mid s, a) \left[ \mathcal{R}(s, a, s') + \gamma \sum_{a'} \pi(a' \mid s') Q^\pi(s', a') \right]$$
3.2 Bellman Optimality Equations
For the optimal functions:
$$V^(s) = \max_a \sum_{s'} \mathcal{P}(s' \mid s, a) \left[ \mathcal{R}(s, a, s') + \gamma V^(s') \right]$$
$$Q^(s, a) = \sum_{s'} \mathcal{P}(s' \mid s, a) \left[ \mathcal{R}(s, a, s') + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^(s', a') \right]$$
These are nonlinear equations (due to the max), so they cannot be solved analytically in general. Solving them is the central algorithmic challenge of RL.
4. Q-Learning
4.1 Temporal Difference Learning
Model-free RL methods estimate value functions without knowing $\mathcal{P}$ or $\mathcal{R}$. Temporal Difference (TD) learning updates estimates using the Bellman backup:
$$V(s_t) \leftarrow V(s_t) + \alpha \underbrace{\left[ r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t) \right]}_{\text{TD error } \delta_t}$$
The TD error $\delta_t$ measures how wrong our current estimate is.
4.2 Q-Learning Algorithm
Q-learning (Watkins & Dayan, 1992) directly estimates $Q^*$:
$$Q(s_t, a_t) \leftarrow Q(s_t, a_t) + \alpha \left[ r_t + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1}, a') - Q(s_t, a_t) \right]$$
This is an off-policy algorithm: the update uses $\max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1}, a')$ (optimal policy) regardless of what action was actually taken next.
import numpy as npimport gymnasium as gymdef q_learning(env_name="FrozenLake-v1", n_episodes=10000,               alpha=0.1, gamma=0.99, epsilon=0.1):    env = gym.make(env_name)    n_states  = env.observation_space.n    n_actions = env.action_space.n    Q = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))    rewards_per_episode = []    for episode in range(n_episodes):        state, _ = env.reset()        total_reward = 0        done = False        while not done:            # Epsilon-greedy action selection            if np.random.rand() < epsilon:                action = env.action_space.sample()        # explore            else:                action = np.argmax(Q[state])              # exploit            next_state, reward, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(action)            done = terminated or truncated            # Q-learning update (Bellman optimality)            td_target = reward + gamma * np.max(Q[next_state]) * (not done)            td_error  = td_target - Q[state, action]            Q[state, action] += alpha * td_error            state = next_state            total_reward += reward        rewards_per_episode.append(total_reward)    env.close()    return Q, rewards_per_episodeQ, rewards = q_learning()print(f"Average reward (last 1000 episodes): {np.mean(rewards[-1000:]):.3f}")
4.3 Deep Q-Networks (DQN)
For large state spaces (e.g., pixel observations), tabular Q-tables are infeasible. DQN (Mnih et al., 2015) approximates $Q^*(s, a; \theta)$ with a neural network.
Two key innovations that make training stable:
* Experience replay: Store transitions $(s, a, r, s')$ in a replay buffer; sample mini-batches randomly to break temporal correlations.
* Target network: Use a separate, periodically-updated network $Q^-(s', a'; \theta^-)$ for the TD target to reduce non-stationarity.
import torchimport torch.nn as nnfrom collections import deque, namedtupleimport randomTransition = namedtuple('Transition', ['state', 'action', 'reward', 'next_state', 'done'])class ReplayBuffer:    def __init__(self, capacity=10000):        self.buffer = deque(maxlen=capacity)    def push(self, *args):        self.buffer.append(Transition(*args))    def sample(self, batch_size):        return random.sample(self.buffer, batch_size)    def __len__(self):        return len(self.buffer)class DQN(nn.Module):    def __init__(self, state_dim, action_dim, hidden=128):        super().__init__()        self.net = nn.Sequential(            nn.Linear(state_dim, hidden), nn.ReLU(),            nn.Linear(hidden, hidden),   nn.ReLU(),            nn.Linear(hidden, action_dim)        )    def forward(self, x):        return self.net(x)
5. Policy Gradient Methods
5.1 The Policy Gradient Theorem
Value-based methods (Q-learning, DQN) learn a value function and derive a policy from it. Policy gradient methods directly optimize the policy by gradient ascent on the expected return:
$$J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}{\pi\theta}[G_t]$$
The policy gradient theorem (Sutton et al., 1999) gives:
$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}{\pi\theta} \left[ \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) \cdot G_t \right]$$
Intuition: increase the log-probability of actions that led to high returns; decrease it for actions that led to low returns.
5.2 REINFORCE Algorithm
REINFORCE (Williams, 1992) is the simplest policy gradient algorithm. It collects full episode trajectories and uses Monte Carlo returns:
import torchimport torch.nn as nnimport torch.optim as optimimport gymnasium as gymclass PolicyNetwork(nn.Module):    def __init__(self, state_dim, action_dim):        super().__init__()        self.net = nn.Sequential(            nn.Linear(state_dim, 128), nn.ReLU(),            nn.Linear(128, action_dim)        )    def forward(self, x):        return torch.softmax(self.net(x), dim=-1)def reinforce(env_name="CartPole-v1", n_episodes=1000,              gamma=0.99, lr=1e-3):    env = gym.make(env_name)    state_dim  = env.observation_space.shape[0]    action_dim = env.action_space.n    policy    = PolicyNetwork(state_dim, action_dim)    optimizer = optim.Adam(policy.parameters(), lr=lr)    for episode in range(n_episodes):        states, actions, rewards = [], [], []        state, _ = env.reset()        done = False        # Collect full episode trajectory        while not done:            state_t = torch.FloatTensor(state)            probs   = policy(state_t)            dist    = torch.distributions.Categorical(probs)            action  = dist.sample()            next_state, reward, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(action.item())            done = terminated or truncated            states.append(state_t)            actions.append(action)            rewards.append(reward)            state = next_state        # Compute discounted returns        G, returns = 0, []        for r in reversed(rewards):            G = r + gamma * G            returns.insert(0, G)        returns = torch.tensor(returns, dtype=torch.float32)        # Normalize returns (variance reduction)        returns = (returns - returns.mean()) / (returns.std() + 1e-8)        # Policy gradient loss        loss = 0        for state_t, action, G_t in zip(states, actions, returns):            probs  = policy(state_t)            dist   = torch.distributions.Categorical(probs)            loss  -= dist.log_prob(action) * G_t   # negative for gradient ascent        optimizer.zero_grad()        loss.backward()        optimizer.step()    env.close()    return policy
Limitation of REINFORCE: High variance in gradient estimates due to Monte Carlo returns. This makes learning slow and unstable.
5.3 Variance Reduction with Baselines
The policy gradient theorem allows subtracting a baseline $b(s)$ without introducing bias:
$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}{\pi\theta} \left[ \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) \cdot (G_t - b(s_t)) \right]$$
The optimal baseline is the state value function $V^\pi(s_t)$. The quantity $(G_t - V^\pi(s_t))$ is called the advantage $A_t$: how much better was action $a_t$ than average?
$$A_t = G_t - V^\pi(s_t)$$
6. Actor-Critic Methods
6.1 The Actor-Critic Architecture
Actor-critic methods address REINFORCE's high variance by using a value function (the critic) to estimate the baseline, while the actor is the policy being optimized.
* Actor $\pi_\theta(a \mid s)$: the policy, updated via policy gradient
* Critic $V_\phi(s)$: a value function, updated via TD learning
The advantage is estimated as:
$$\hat{A}t = r_t + \gamma V\phi(s_{t+1}) - V_\phi(s_t) \quad \text{(TD advantage)}$$
6.2 A2C: Advantage Actor-Critic
A2C (Mnih et al., 2016) is the synchronous version of A3C. It runs multiple environment instances in parallel, collects trajectories, and updates the network synchronously.
class ActorCritic(nn.Module):    def __init__(self, state_dim, action_dim):        super().__init__()        # Shared feature extractor        self.shared = nn.Sequential(            nn.Linear(state_dim, 256), nn.ReLU(),            nn.Linear(256, 256),       nn.ReLU()        )        # Actor head: outputs action probabilities        self.actor  = nn.Linear(256, action_dim)        # Critic head: outputs state value        self.critic = nn.Linear(256, 1)    def forward(self, x):        features = self.shared(x)        logits   = self.actor(features)        value    = self.critic(features)        return logits, value    def get_action_and_value(self, state):        logits, value = self.forward(state)        dist   = torch.distributions.Categorical(logits=logits)        action = dist.sample()        return action, dist.log_prob(action), dist.entropy(), value.squeeze()
The A2C loss combines actor and critic losses:
$$\mathcal{L}(\theta, \phi) = \underbrace{-\mathbb{E}\left[\log \pi_\theta(a \mid s) \cdot \hat{A}\right]}{\text{actor loss}} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\left[(V\phi(s) - G_t)^2\right]}{\text{critic loss}} - \underbrace{\beta \cdot H(\pi\theta)}_{\text{entropy bonus}}$$
The entropy bonus $H(\pi_\theta) = -\sum_a \pi_\theta(a \mid s) \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)$ encourages exploration.
6.3 A3C: Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic
A3C (Mnih et al., 2016) uses multiple parallel worker threads, each running its own environment and computing gradients asynchronously. Workers push gradients to a global model and pull updated parameters. A2C (synchronous) is simpler and often performs as well on modern hardware with vectorized environments.
Key Concept: On-Policy vs. Off-Policy On-policy methods (REINFORCE, A2C, A3C, PPO) learn from data generated by the current policy. Off-policy methods (Q-learning, DQN, SAC) can learn from data generated by any policy, including older versions or human demonstrations. On-policy methods tend to be more stable but less sample-efficient.
7. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)
7.1 The Problem with Large Policy Updates
In standard policy gradient, large gradient steps can dramatically change the policy, causing:
* Catastrophic forgetting of useful behaviors
* Falling into poor local optima that are hard to escape
* Divergence in training
Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO, Schulman et al., 2015) constrains the KL divergence between old and new policies. However, TRPO requires computing the Fisher information matrix, which is computationally expensive.
7.2 The PPO Clipped Objective
PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) achieves the benefits of TRPO with a simpler, first-order method. Define the probability ratio:
$$r_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t \mid s_t)}$$
The clipped surrogate objective is:
$$\mathcal{L}^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t \left[ \min \left( r_t(\theta) \hat{A}_t, ; \text{clip}(r_t(\theta), 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon) \hat{A}_t \right) \right]$$
The min and clip prevent the policy from making excessively large updates:
* If $\hat{A}_t > 0$: action was good, but don't increase its probability by more than $(1+\epsilon)$ times
* If $\hat{A}_t < 0$: action was bad, but don't decrease its probability by more than $(1-\epsilon)$ times
Typical value: $\epsilon = 0.2$.
7.3 Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE)
PPO typically uses GAE (Schulman et al., 2016) for more accurate advantage estimates. GAE interpolates between TD(0) and Monte Carlo returns:
$$\hat{A}t^{\text{GAE}(\lambda)} = \sum{l=0}^{\infty} (\gamma\lambda)^l \delta_{t+l}$$
where $\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)$ is the TD error. The parameter $\lambda \in [0,1]$ controls bias-variance tradeoff:
* $\lambda = 0$: $\hat{A}_t = \delta_t$ (TD advantage, low variance, high bias)
* $\lambda = 1$: $\hat{A}_t = G_t - V(s_t)$ (Monte Carlo, low bias, high variance)
7.4 PPO Full Algorithm
import torchimport torch.nn as nnimport torch.optim as optimimport numpy as npimport gymnasium as gymclass PPOAgent:    def __init__(self, state_dim, action_dim,                 lr=3e-4, clip_eps=0.2, gamma=0.99,                 lam=0.95, n_epochs=10, batch_size=64):        self.clip_eps   = clip_eps        self.gamma      = gamma        self.lam        = lam        self.n_epochs   = n_epochs        self.batch_size = batch_size        self.ac        = ActorCritic(state_dim, action_dim)        self.optimizer = optim.Adam(self.ac.parameters(), lr=lr)    def compute_gae(self, rewards, values, dones, last_value):        """Compute Generalized Advantage Estimation."""        advantages = np.zeros(len(rewards), dtype=np.float32)        last_gae   = 0.0        for t in reversed(range(len(rewards))):            if t == len(rewards) - 1:                next_val = last_value            else:                next_val = values[t + 1]            delta       = rewards[t] + self.gamma * next_val * (1 - dones[t]) - values[t]            last_gae    = delta + self.gamma * self.lam * (1 - dones[t]) * last_gae            advantages[t] = last_gae        returns = advantages + values        return advantages, returns    def update(self, states, actions, log_probs_old, returns, advantages):        """Perform multiple epochs of mini-batch PPO updates."""        states      = torch.FloatTensor(states)        actions     = torch.LongTensor(actions)        log_probs_old = torch.FloatTensor(log_probs_old)        returns     = torch.FloatTensor(returns)        advantages  = torch.FloatTensor(advantages)        # Normalize advantages        advantages  = (advantages - advantages.mean()) / (advantages.std() + 1e-8)        n = len(states)        indices = np.arange(n)        for _ in range(self.n_epochs):            np.random.shuffle(indices)            for start in range(0, n, self.batch_size):                idx = indices[start : start + self.batch_size]                logits, values = self.ac(states[idx])                dist           = torch.distributions.Categorical(logits=logits)                log_probs_new  = dist.log_prob(actions[idx])                entropy        = dist.entropy()                # PPO clipped ratio                ratio          = (log_probs_new - log_probs_old[idx]).exp()                surr1          = ratio * advantages[idx]                surr2          = torch.clamp(ratio, 1 - self.clip_eps,                                                    1 + self.clip_eps) * advantages[idx]                actor_loss     = -torch.min(surr1, surr2).mean()                # Critic loss (clipped value loss is optional but common)                critic_loss    = 0.5 * (returns[idx] - values.squeeze()).pow(2).mean()                # Total loss                loss = actor_loss + 0.5 * critic_loss - 0.01 * entropy.mean()                self.optimizer.zero_grad()                loss.backward()                nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(self.ac.parameters(), 0.5)                self.optimizer.step()
7.5 PPO Hyperparameters
Hyperparameter | Typical Value | Effect
clip_eps (ε) | 0.1–0.3 | Smaller = more conservative updates
gamma (γ) | 0.99 | Larger = more far-sighted
lam (λ) | 0.95 | Controls GAE bias-variance trade-off
n_epochs | 4–10 | More epochs = better data utilization, risk of overfit
lr | 3e-4 | Standard Adam learning rate
batch_size | 32–256 | Mini-batch size for updates
rollout_length | 128–2048 | Steps per environment before update
8. Exploration vs. Exploitation
8.1 The Fundamental Tension
An agent must balance:
* Exploitation: Use current knowledge to get the best known reward
* Exploration: Try new actions that might reveal better rewards
This is the exploration-exploitation dilemma. An agent that only exploits gets stuck in local optima; one that only explores never benefits from what it has learned.
8.2 Exploration Strategies
ε-greedy: With probability ε, take a random action; otherwise exploit. Simple but crude — treats all unexplored actions equally.
ε-decay: Start with high exploration (ε = 1.0) and decay it over time.
epsilon = max(epsilon_min, epsilon * epsilon_decay)
Boltzmann/Softmax exploration: Sample actions proportionally to their estimated value:
$$P(a \mid s) = \frac{\exp(Q(s,a) / \tau)}{\sum_{a'} \exp(Q(s,a') / \tau)}$$
Temperature $\tau$ controls randomness: high $\tau$ = uniform (explore), low $\tau$ = greedy (exploit).
Entropy regularization (used in SAC and A2C/PPO): Add $\beta \cdot H(\pi)$ to the objective. The policy naturally explores by maintaining high entropy.
Upper Confidence Bound (UCB): Choose the action that maximizes optimism under uncertainty:
$$a_t = \arg\max_a \left[ Q(s, a) + c \sqrt{\frac{\ln t}{N(s, a)}} \right]$$
where $N(s, a)$ is the number of times action $a$ was taken from state $s$.
Curiosity-driven exploration (Pathak et al., 2017): Add an intrinsic reward based on prediction error — the agent is rewarded for visiting states it cannot yet predict.
9. Reward Shaping
9.1 The Sparse Reward Problem
In many real tasks, rewards are sparse: a robot only gets a reward when it picks up an object, and gets nothing otherwise. This makes learning extremely slow — the agent must stumble upon the reward by chance.
Reward shaping adds auxiliary rewards to guide learning without changing the optimal policy.
9.2 Potential-Based Reward Shaping
Ng et al. (1999) proved that adding a shaping reward of the form:
$$F(s, a, s') = \gamma \Phi(s') - \Phi(s)$$
where $\Phi$ is any potential function, does not change the optimal policy. This is called potential-based shaping.
# Example: reward shaping for reaching a goaldef shaped_reward(state, next_state, original_reward, goal_pos):    """Add reward proportional to progress toward goal."""    dist_curr = np.linalg.norm(state[:2] - goal_pos)    dist_next = np.linalg.norm(next_state[:2] - goal_pos)    shaping = gamma * (-dist_next) - (-dist_curr)   # Phi(s) = -distance    return original_reward + shaping
9.3 Dangers of Reward Shaping
Poorly designed reward shaping can lead to reward hacking: the agent finds unexpected ways to maximize the shaped reward without accomplishing the intended task. A classic example: a boat racing game where the agent learned to spin in circles collecting turbo boosts rather than completing laps (Amodei et al., 2016).
Key Concept: Goodhart's Law in RL "Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes." Reward functions are proxies for what we truly want — and agents will exploit misalignments between the proxy and the true objective.

import gymnasium as gymfrom gymnasium import spacesimport numpy as npclass GridWorldEnv(gym.Env):    """A simple NxN grid world with a goal position."""    metadata = {"render_modes": ["human", "ansi"]}    def __init__(self, size=5):        self.size = size        self.observation_space = spaces.Box(            low=0, high=size - 1, shape=(2,), dtype=np.int32        )        self.action_space = spaces.Discrete(4)  # up, down, left, right        self._action_to_dir = {            0: np.array([0,  1]),   # right            1: np.array([0, -1]),   # left            2: np.array([1,  0]),   # down            3: np.array([-1, 0]),   # up        }    def reset(self, seed=None, options=None):        super().reset(seed=seed)        self._agent_pos = np.array([0, 0])        self._goal_pos  = np.array([self.size - 1, self.size - 1])        return self._agent_pos.copy(), {}    def step(self, action):        direction        = self._action_to_dir[action]        self._agent_pos  = np.clip(self._agent_pos + direction,                                   0, self.size - 1)        terminated       = np.array_equal(self._agent_pos, self._goal_pos)        reward           = 1.0 if terminated else -0.01        return self._agent_pos.copy(), reward, terminated, False, {}
